format.melody: Bars separated by |. A note is letter + optional # or b (## / bb) + octave + duration (w h q e s = whole, half, quarter, eighth, sixteenth), then optional . (dotted) and ~ (tied to the next note of the same pitch). r + duration is a rest. Middle C is C4. Accidentals are the sounding pitch, not relative to the key signature. If the tune has a pickup, the first bar holds only the pickup beats.
format.chords: One entry per full bar (no chord for the pickup), separated by |. Several chords in a bar split it evenly, or give beats with Chord:beats. Qualities: (major) m 7 m7 maj7 dim dim7 m7b5 6 m6 aug sus4 9.
format.staves: Optional written accompaniment. Use staves.bass with a label and events. Each event has s (start in quarter-note beats from the beginning), d (duration in quarter-note beats), and n (pitch or space-separated pitches, with octaves).
format.band: Default play-along style: swing, twobeat, rock, bossa, ballad (4/4); waltz, jazzwaltz, ballad (3/4); jig (6/8).
format.liner: Liner notes shown under the sheet: origins (where the song comes from), tradition (how it is traditionally played), listen (recordings worth hearing), try (a way to practise that style here). Keep facts sourced and hedge anything uncertain.
format.chordsOnly: True for harmony practice charts without a melody. Rest bars preserve the form; section labels mark the chorus. Changes are simplified practice arrangements and may differ from a recording.
format.category: Built-in library section. Use one of: Traditional & folk, Hymns & spirituals, Classical themes, Seasonal songs, Early popular & ragtime, Jazz standards, Jazz practice charts, Original exercises.
format.seasonalGroup: Holiday or season for a seasonal song. Use Christmas (Sacred), Christmas (Secular), Hanukkah, Passover, New Year, or Spring.
format.culture: Cultural origin of the seasonal song or setting in this book.
format.sortYear: Seasonal chronology. Use the composition year when known, otherwise the year of an early publication, collection, recording or performance. Name the event in year. Use null for undated tunes, and use the start of the decade for decade-only dates.
format.lyrics: Optional public-domain lyric block for vocal sight-reading: { year, credit, verses: [{ mark, label?, text }] }. Bars in text are separated by |; hyphenated words split across notes (Twin- kle), _ holds a melisma onto the next note, * skips a sung note, and ‿ joins two syllables onto one note.

tunes.title: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star
tunes.composer: French folk melody (“Ah! vous dirai-je, maman”)
tunes.year: Melody printed 1761 · words by Jane Taylor, 1806
tunes.melody: C4q C4q G4q G4q | A4q A4q G4h | F4q F4q E4q E4q | D4q D4q C4h | G4q G4q F4q F4q | E4q E4q D4h | G4q G4q F4q F4q | E4q E4q D4h | C4q C4q G4q G4q | A4q A4q G4h | F4q F4q E4q E4q | D4q D4q C4h

tunes.about: Mozart wrote twelve variations on this melody (K. 265). Do what he did: keep the chords and change the tune.
tunes.source: Melody as printed in Paris, 1761; public domain everywhere. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: The tune is French. It was printed in Paris in 1761 and sung as “Ah! vous dirai-je, maman,” a child complaining to her mother. In 1806 the English poet Jane Taylor published “The Star,” the poem we now sing as “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star,” in a book of nursery rhymes she wrote with her sister Ann. The same melody carries “Baa, Baa, Black Sheep” and the Alphabet Song, which a Boston publisher copyrighted in 1835. Around 1781 Mozart, then in his twenties in Vienna, wrote twelve piano variations on it (K. 265).
liner.tradition: Because it moves by step and repeats its phrases, it is many musicians’ first tune. The Suzuki violin method opens with “Twinkle Variations,” where students play the same melody in a series of different rhythms before they learn anything else. Mozart’s variations show the opposite end: the tune stays in the background while runs, minor-key turns and ornaments decorate it. Teachers use it to practise call and response, rhythm games and transposition.
listen: Mozart, Twelve Variations on “Ah vous dirai-je, Maman,” K. 265 (any piano recording)
Suzuki Violin School, Book 1: “Twinkle Variations”
liner.try: Play it with each Rhythm setting in turn, the way Suzuki students do. Then pick Upside down and ask whether it is still the same tune.

lyrics.credit: Words by Jane Taylor, “The Star” (1806, public domain)

verses.text: Twin- kle, twin- kle, | lit- tle star, | How I won- der | what you are! | Up a- bove the | world so high, | Like a dia- mond | in the sky. | Twin- kle, twin- kle, | lit- tle star, | How I won- der | what you are!

tunes.title: Frère Jacques
tunes.melody: F4q G4q A4q F4q | F4q G4q A4q F4q | A4q Bb4q C5h | A4q Bb4q C5h | C5e D5e C5e Bb4e A4q F4q | C5e D5e C5e Bb4e A4q F4q | F4q C4q F4h | F4q C4q F4h
tunes.about: A round: a second group starts the same tune two bars later and it still fits. Mahler turned it into a slow minor-key march in his First Symphony (1888). Try “Upside down” for a melody that sounds almost as natural.
tunes.source: Traditional; public domain. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: A French round about Brother John, a friar who has overslept and missed ringing the morning bells (“sonnez les matines”). The oldest known copy is a Paris manuscript from about 1780. Some researchers have linked it to the composer Jean-Philippe Rameau, but nobody knows for certain who wrote it. It travelled with the words translated: “Are You Sleeping, Brother John?” in English, “Bruder Jakob” in German, and “Two Tigers” in Chinese.
liner.tradition: It is built to be sung as a round: up to four groups enter two bars apart and the parts fit together because every phrase outlines the same chord. In 1888 Gustav Mahler turned it into a slow minor-key funeral march in the third movement of his First Symphony, opening with a solo double bass. Playground versions speed up each time through; choirs use it to teach singing in parts.
listen: Mahler, Symphony No. 1, third movement (the minor-key round on solo double bass)
liner.try: Split the room into groups and sing it as a round over the band. Then try Upside down: the inverted tune still works as a round.

lyrics.credit: Traditional French round and English translation (public domain)

tunes.about: Beethoven’s tune moves almost entirely by step, one scale note at a time. Try “Chord tones” and “Skeleton” to hear the harmony underneath it.
tunes.source: Beethoven, Symphony No. 9, Op. 125 (1824), in its original key of D; public domain. Chords simplified for this page.

liner.origins: Beethoven set Friedrich Schiller’s poem “An die Freude” (1785) in the finale of his Ninth Symphony, first performed in Vienna on 7 May 1824. He had sketched settings of the poem for decades. By the premiere he was almost completely deaf; the story goes that a singer had to turn him round to see the audience applauding. It was the first symphony by a major composer to bring singers and a chorus into the final movement.
liner.tradition: The orchestra introduces the tune quietly in the cellos and basses, then passes it up through the orchestra before the voices take it. Listen for the famous jolt in the second half: one note arrives a beat early, tied across the bar line. The melody became the hymn “Joyful, Joyful, We Adore Thee” (1907) and, without words, the anthem of Europe. Leonard Bernstein conducted the symphony in Berlin at Christmas 1989, after the Wall came down, and changed the word “Freude” (joy) to “Freiheit” (freedom).
listen: Beethoven, Symphony No. 9, fourth movement (the theme first appears in the low strings)
Leonard Bernstein, Berlin, December 1989 (“Ode to Freedom”)
liner.try: Play it slowly in Melody + click, then switch to Chord tones and Skeleton to hear how little the harmony moves under a tune that moves by step.

lyrics.credit: English hymn words by Henry van Dyke (1907, public domain)

liner.origins: Sarah Josepha Hale printed the poem in 1830. It appeared with music in school songbooks soon afterward; the familiar short melody is now taught in many different keys.
liner.tradition: Teachers use the tune to introduce steps and repeats. The whole melody fits on four notes, so students can sing, play, and transpose it before reading a large staff range.
listen: Sing the familiar nursery tune before pressing Play; compare the final phrase with the first.
liner.try: Turn on note names, play the melody, then transpose from C to F and find the same four-note pattern.

tunes.title: Old MacDonald Had a Farm
tunes.year: Printed as “Ohio” in 1917 · folk roots older
tunes.melody: G4q G4q G4q D4q | E4q E4q D4h | B4q B4q A4q A4q | G4h. D4q | G4q G4q G4q D4q | E4q E4q D4h | B4q B4q A4q A4q | G4h. D4e D4e | G4q G4q G4q D4e D4e | G4q G4q G4h | G4e G4e G4q G4e G4e G4q | G4e G4e G4e G4e G4q G4q | G4q G4q G4q D4q | E4q E4q D4h | B4q B4q A4q A4q | G4w

tunes.about: The middle of the song sits on one note (G) for four bars while the animal sounds pile up. Every verse adds a new animal; the first, second and last lines never change.
tunes.source: Traditional; public domain. Melody as commonly sung in the US; an early print is “Ohio” in F. T. Nettleingham’s Tommy’s Tunes (London, 1917). Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: Nobody knows who first sang it. Farmyard songs listing animals and their noises are much older, but a version with the “E-I-E-I-O” refrain was printed in 1917 in Tommy’s Tunes, a collection of songs British soldiers sang in the First World War, as “Ohio” (“Old Macdougal had a farm, in Ohio-i-o”). Folk singers and children’s records spread it through the 1920s and after, and the farmer’s name settled into MacDonald.
liner.tradition: It is a cumulative song: each verse brings a new animal, and in many classrooms the singers repeat every earlier animal’s sound too, so the middle section grows longer and longer. Children choose the animals and invent the noises, which makes it a favourite for call and response.
listen: Any children’s songbook or classroom recording; compare how many animals each one stacks up.
liner.try: Play it with the band, then sing a new animal each time through. Notice that the four “here a moo, there a moo” bars are all on G: try singing them on the D below instead.

lyrics.credit: Traditional words (public domain); animals vary from singer to singer

tunes.title: Row, Row, Row Your Boat
tunes.composer: Traditional round (tune often credited to Eliphalet Oram Lyte)
tunes.melody: C4q. C4q. | C4q D4e E4q. | E4q D4e E4q F4e | G4h. | C5e C5e C5e G4e G4e G4e | E4e E4e E4e C4e C4e C4e | G4q F4e E4q D4e | C4h.

tunes.about: A round: a second group starts from the top when the first reaches bar 3, and it fits because nearly every bar is the C chord. The “merrily” bars walk down a C chord, C–G–E–C.
tunes.source: Traditional; public domain. Tune as printed in The Franklin Square Song Collection (1881). Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: The words appeared in print in the United States in 1852, sung to a different tune. The melody everyone knows now was printed in 1881 in The Franklin Square Song Collection, where it is credited to Eliphalet Oram Lyte; whether Lyte composed it or arranged an existing tune is not certain.
liner.tradition: It is sung as a round, usually by two to four groups who enter two bars apart. It is one of the first part-songs children learn, because every entry lands on the same chord and the parts never clash. The swaying 6/8 rhythm imitates the pull of the oars.
listen: Any classroom round: listen for the moment the second group’s “Row, row” lines up under the first group’s “gently down the stream.”
liner.try: Play the melody, then split the room and start a second group at bar 3. Clap the 6/8 pulse in two big beats per bar (ONE-and-a TWO-and-a) while you sing.

lyrics.credit: Traditional words (printed 1852, public domain)

verses.text: Row, row, | row your boat | gent- ly down the | stream. | Mer- ri- ly mer- ri- ly | mer- ri- ly mer- ri- ly | life is but a | dream.

tunes.title: The Wheels on the Bus
tunes.composer: Words usually credited to Verna Hills · traditional tune
tunes.melody: C4q | F4q F4e F4e F4q A4q | C5q A4q F4h | G4q E4q C4h | C5q A4q F4q C4q | F4q F4e F4e F4q A4q | C5q A4q F4h | G4h C4q C4q | F4h. rq

tunes.about: Eight bars and only two chords. Bars 2–4 sing the same words three times, stepping up and down an F chord (C–A–F) and then a C chord (G–E–C).
tunes.source: Words usually credited to Verna Hills, American Childhood (1939), and sung as a traditional song; the tune is related to “Here We Go Round the Mulberry Bush.” Melody as commonly sung in US classrooms. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: The song is usually traced to the American writer Verna Hills, whose words were printed in 1939 in the teachers’ magazine American Childhood. The tune is close to the old English singing game “Here We Go Round the Mulberry Bush.” Since then it has been sung in nursery schools around the world, often with new verses made up on the spot.
liner.tradition: Every verse is a different part of the bus and a sound or a hand movement: wheels rolling, a horn beeping, wipers swishing, doors opening and shutting. Children act out each verse, so it is a movement song as much as a singing one.
listen: Any classroom or nursery-school recording; listen for how many different verses each one uses.
liner.try: Sing a verse, then let someone choose the next part of the bus and its sound. Keep it in rhythm: the new sound has to fit three notes.

lyrics.credit: Words usually credited to Verna Hills (1939); verses vary from singer to singer

tunes.title: The Itsy Bitsy Spider
tunes.melody: G3e | C4q C4e C4q D4e | E4q. E4q E4e | D4q C4e D4q E4e | C4q. rq E4e | E4q F4e G4q. | G4q F4e E4q F4e | G4q. E4q C4e | C4q D4e E4q. | E4q D4e C4q D4e | E4q C4q. G3e | G3e C4e C4e C4q D4e | E4q. E4q E4e | D4q C4e D4q E4e | C4q. rq.

tunes.about: Four phrases, and the spider climbs each time: the rain phrase starts on E and rises to G, then the sun phrase drops back to C. Counting in 6/8 means two big swaying beats per bar.
tunes.source: Traditional; public domain. Words printed by 1910; melody as commonly sung in US classrooms. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: Nobody knows who made it up. An early printed version of the words appears in 1910, in a travel book about Baja California, with a rougher adjective for the spider than “itsy bitsy.” It has been sung in many versions since (“Incy Wincy Spider” in Britain and Australia).
liner.tradition: It is a finger play: the hands climb the spout, the fingers fall as rain, the arms make the sun, and the spider climbs again. Many classes also sing a “great big hairy spider” verse, low and slow, to show that the same tune can sound completely different.
listen: Any classroom recording; compare the British “Incy Wincy Spider” words with the American ones.
liner.try: Do the hand movements while the band plays. Then lower the tempo, pick a low octave and sing it as the great big spider.

lyrics.credit: Traditional words (public domain)

verses.text: The | it- sy bit- sy | spi- der went | up the wa- ter | spout. Down | came the rain | and washed the spi- | der out. Out | came the sun | and dried up all | the rain. And | the it- sy bit- sy | spi- der went | up the spout a- | gain.

tunes.about: The same minor-key march as “When Johnny Comes Marching Home” (also in this book), with new words. Each verse counts up one number and finds a rhyme for it.
tunes.source: Traditional children’s words, public domain; tune from Patrick Gilmore’s When Johnny Comes Marching Home (1863), adapted here to fit the words. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: The tune is Patrick Gilmore’s Civil War march “When Johnny Comes Marching Home” (1863). Children’s camps and schools later gave it new words about a line of ants marching underground out of the rain. Who wrote the ant words, and when, is not known.
liner.tradition: It is a counting song: verse one is “one by one, the little one stops to suck his thumb,” and each new verse adds one and a new rhyme (two: tie his shoe; three: climb a tree; four: shut the door…). Singers usually march in place, and the “Boom! Boom! Boom!” at the end is stamped.
listen: Compare it with “When Johnny Comes Marching Home” in this book: same tune, very different mood.
liner.try: March to the two big beats in each bar. Then open “When Johnny Comes Marching Home” and find the bars where the tunes match note for note.

tunes.title: Au clair de la lune
tunes.year: Traditional melody · printed in 19th-century song collections
tunes.melody: C4e C4e C4e D4e E4q D4q | C4e E4e D4e D4e C4h | C4e C4e C4e D4e E4q D4q | C4e E4e D4e D4e C4h | D4e D4e D4e D4e A3q A3q | D4e C4e B3e A3e G3h | C4e C4e C4e D4e E4q D4q | C4e E4e D4e D4e C4h
tunes.about: Two phrases return almost exactly; the middle phrase drops below middle C. Notice how repetition makes an eight-bar tune easy to remember.

liner.origins: This French song addresses Pierrot by moonlight. Versions circulated orally before appearing in printed children's song collections; the tune and wording vary between versions.
liner.tradition: Its opening phrase repeats, then a lower answering phrase leads back home. That makes it useful for hearing the difference between the main idea and a contrasting middle.
listen: Sing the first French line, “Au clair de la lune,” and listen for that same phrase returning.
liner.try: Loop bars 1–2, then bars 5–6. Compare where the second phrase sits on the staff.

lyrics.credit: Traditional French song (public domain)

liner.origins: This Shaker song is generally attributed to Elder Joseph Brackett and dates to 1848. Its verse celebrates simplicity, freedom, and turning back to the right place.
liner.tradition: The tune's even pulse and circling phrases suit a communal dance. Aaron Copland later used it in Appalachian Spring, but this lead sheet follows the older song rather than his orchestral setting.
listen: A traditional unaccompanied Shaker-style singing of “Simple Gifts”
Aaron Copland, Appalachian Spring (listen for the borrowed melody)
liner.try: Sing the pickup before you press Play. Loop bars 9–12 and notice how the longer notes change the phrase's energy.

lyrics.credit: Shaker song attributed to Elder Joseph Brackett (1848, public domain)

verses.text: ’Tis the | gift to be sim- ple, ’tis the | gift to be free, ’tis the | gift to come down | where we ought _ to be, | When we find our- selves in the | place just right, ’twill | be in the val- ley of | love and de- light. | When true sim- | pli- ci- ty is gained, To | bow and to bend we | shan’t be a- shamed, To | turn, turn will | be our de- light, Till by | turn- ing, turn- ing we | come ’round right.

liner.origins: James Lord Pierpont published the song in 1857 under the title “The One Horse Open Sleigh.” The chorus later became better known as “Jingle Bells.”
liner.tradition: Its repeated notes make the pulse easy to feel, while the quick final phrase gives students a reason to count eighth and sixteenth notes carefully.

liner.try: Play the first two bars with a steady click. Then mute the melody and see whether you can keep the repeated B notes evenly spaced.

tunes.about: All twelve days, written out. Every gift has its own bar, so give each one to a different player and count when your bar comes back. The last verse has twelve entrances.
tunes.source: Traditional English carol in its usual 20th-century form (Frederic Austin, 1909). Melody follows the BBC Singing Together (1970) transcription at https://abcnotation.com/tunePage?a=trillian.mit.edu/~jc/music/abc/mirror/folkinfo.org/Twelve_Days_of_Christmas/0000 , with days 6–12 and chords checked against Colin Hume’s ABC (https://abcnotation.com/tunePage?a=colinhume.com/ABC.txt/1432). The gift bars are three beats long in the original; here each is held one beat longer so the song fits a steady 4/4.

liner.origins: Leontovych arranged a Ukrainian shchedrivka, a New Year well-wishing song. The Ukrainian Institute dates its first performance to 1916 and its Carnegie Hall performance to 1922.
liner.tradition: The Ukrainian song belongs to New Year traditions; the familiar English Christmas title came later. In the choral setting, several voices layer around the repeated figure.
listen: Listen to Shchedryk in Ukrainian, such as the Ukrainian Children’s Choir Shchedryk, and follow the repeating figure through the different voices.
liner.try: Loop the first four bars as an ostinato. Then practise the scale passage slowly; its F-sharp leads upward to G.

tunes.title: When the Saints Go Marching In
tunes.year: Printed by 1896 · a New Orleans jazz standard

tunes.about: Starts with a three-note pickup before bar 1. New Orleans bands play it in a “two-beat” feel: bass on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. Switch the band to Swing and play with “Push” to hear it get jazzier.
tunes.source: Traditional spiritual; public domain. Lead sheet written for this page from the traditional melody.

liner.origins: An African American spiritual about the hope of joining the saints in heaven. It was sung in Black churches in the South long before anyone wrote it down, and similar gospel hymns were printed in the 1890s. Louis Armstrong’s 1938 recording turned it into a jazz hit, and it became the tune most associated with New Orleans.
liner.tradition: In a New Orleans jazz funeral the brass band plays hymns slowly as a dirge on the way to the cemetery, then breaks into a fast, joyful “Saints” on the way back while the “second line” of neighbours dances behind. Bands play it in a two-beat feel and pass the melody between trumpet, clarinet and trombone, which play different lines at once (collective improvisation). Crowds sing along and answer the leader’s lines.
listen: Louis Armstrong and His Orchestra (1938)
Any New Orleans brass band, such as the Preservation Hall Jazz Band or the Dirty Dozen Brass Band
liner.try: Play it once as a dirge (Ballad band, slow tempo), then go to Two-beat at a quick tempo, the way a funeral band turns for home.

tunes.about: In 3/4 time with a one-beat pickup. The melody uses only five notes of the scale (a pentatonic scale), which is why it works on so many instruments. Try the Jazz waltz band.
tunes.source: “New Britain” as printed in Columbian Harmony (1829); public domain. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: John Newton, an English sailor who had worked in the Atlantic slave trade and later became a clergyman and opponent of it, wrote the words for a New Year’s Day sermon in 1773. They were published in Olney Hymns in 1779. The tune, called “New Britain,” is an American folk melody from the shape-note singing books of the early 1800s. William Walker joined Newton’s words to it in his book Southern Harmony (1835), and that pairing stuck.
liner.tradition: It is sung many ways: in four-part shape-note harmony, in the slow “lined-out” style of African American churches where a leader calls each line and the congregation answers with long, ornamented notes, and with gospel melisma (many notes on one syllable) as Mahalia Jackson and Aretha Franklin sang it. Its five-note scale fits the bagpipes, and a pipe band version topped the British charts in 1972. Singers stretch the tempo freely.

Judy Collins (1970, a cappella)
The Royal Scots Dragoon Guards (1972, bagpipes)
liner.try: Use the Ballad band at a slow tempo and decorate each long note with a turn. Then switch to Jazz waltz to hear it as a jazz tune.

liner.origins: Julia Ward Howe wrote new words for a tune already sung as “John Brown’s Body.” Her poem appeared in The Atlantic Monthly in February 1862, during the American Civil War. William Steffe is commonly credited with the older camp-meeting melody, though the tune’s early history is not fully settled.
liner.tradition: The song joins three long verse lines to the repeated “Glory, glory, hallelujah” refrain, sung to the same tune as “John Brown’s Body.” Singers often broaden the last line, “His truth is marching on.”
listen: Compare this lead sheet with the Library of Congress 1862 printed score

tunes.melody: A4q | C5h D5q | E5q. F#5e E5q | D5h B4q | G4q. A4e B4q | C5h A4q | A4q. G#4e A4q | B4h G#4q | E4h A4q | C5h D5q | E5q. F#5e E5q | D5h B4q | G4q. A4e B4q | C5q. B4e A4q | G#4q. F#4e G#4q | A4h. | A4h r4q

tunes.about: A minor key. The G♯ is borrowed from the harmonic minor scale to lead back to A. The same tune became the carol “What Child Is This?” (1865).
tunes.source: Traditional English tune; public domain. Lead sheet and chords written for this page.

liner.origins: A ballad called “A New Northern Dittye of the Lady Greene Sleeves” was registered in London in 1580. A popular legend says Henry VIII wrote it for Anne Boleyn, but the tune is built on Italian chord patterns (the romanesca and passamezzo antico) that reached England after Henry died. Shakespeare mentions it twice in The Merry Wives of Windsor, so audiences of the 1590s already knew it.
liner.tradition: In the Renaissance it was played on lute and viols, with players adding new variations over the repeating chords each time round. In 1865 William Chatterton Dix wrote the Christmas words “What Child Is This?” to it. Ralph Vaughan Williams used it in his opera Sir John in Love, and his Fantasia on Greensleeves (1934) made it an orchestral favourite. John Coltrane recorded it in 1961 as a modal jazz waltz. Players choose between the raised and plain sixth and seventh notes of the minor scale, which changes its colour.

tunes.year: Words by Robert Burns, 1788 · tune printed 1799

tunes.about: Only five notes: F G A C D, the major pentatonic scale. The dotted “long-short” rhythm is a Scottish fingerprint. Try “Short-long” to hear the Scotch snap.
tunes.source: Traditional Scottish tune; public domain. Verse only. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: “Auld lang syne” is Scots for “old long since”: days gone by. In 1788 Robert Burns sent the poem to a collection of Scottish songs, saying he had taken it down from an old man’s singing, though he probably added verses himself. It was first printed with a different melody; the tune everyone sings now was paired with the words in George Thomson’s Select Scottish Airs in 1799.
liner.tradition: It is sung at Hogmanay, the Scottish New Year, and then around the world at midnight on 31 December. Singers stand in a circle holding hands, and on the last verse cross their arms and join hands with the people on either side. In the United States, Guy Lombardo’s band played it on New Year’s radio and TV broadcasts from 1929 for nearly fifty years. In Japan the same tune, as “Hotaru no Hikari,” is sung at graduations and played when shops close.
listen: Any Hogmanay recording with pipes and voices
Guy Lombardo and His Royal Canadians (New Year’s broadcast version)
liner.try: Try the Short–long rhythm to hear the Scotch snap, a short note on the beat followed by a long one, which is a fingerprint of Scottish fiddle music.

liner.origins: The farewell text has Scottish roots, while the familiar air has circulated in Irish tradition. liner.tradition: Often sung at the close of a gathering, with a restrained opening and a broader refrain. Singers may stretch the final line, so the written rhythm is a starting point rather than a fixed performance.

liner.origins: The tune circulated around Britain, Ireland and North America under several titles. A nineteenth-century manuscript already records “The Irish Washerwoman”; exact origins are debated. Tune history and variants: https://ibiblio.org/fiddlers/IP_IZ.htm
liner.tradition: A double jig has six eighth notes per bar, grouped three plus three. Sessions commonly repeat the eight-bar A and B strains (AABB) before moving to another tune.
listen: Listen to a traditional fiddle or whistle performance and tap only the two main pulses in each bar.

tunes.title: Classroom Blues
tunes.composer: Original riff for ClassroomOS (free to use)
tunes.melody: C4e Eb4e E4q G4q r4q | A4q G4e Eb4e C4q r4q | r4q C5q Bb4q G4q | C5h r4h | F4e Ab4e A4q C5q r4q | D5q C5e Ab4e F4q r4q | C4e Eb4e E4q G4q r4q | A4q G4e Eb4e C4q r4q | G4e Bb4e B4q D5q r4q | F4e Ab4e A4q C5q r4q | C4e Eb4e E4q G4q r4q | r4q G4q F4q D4q
tunes.about: The 12-bar blues: four bars on I, two on IV, two on I, then V, IV, I, V. The riff moves to fit each chord. Use Trade fours to improvise your own riff in the empty bars.
tunes.source: Written for this site; free for any classroom to copy, play and change.

liner.origins: This riff was written for ClassroomOS, but the form is about 120 years old. The blues grew in African American communities in the Deep South in the late 1800s out of work songs, field hollers and spirituals. By the 1910s songwriters such as W. C. Handy were publishing blues in the 12-bar form you see here: three four-bar lines over the I, IV and V chords.
liner.tradition: Blues lyrics often follow an AAB pattern: a line, the same line again, then an answer. Instruments do the same with riffs, short phrases repeated and moved to fit each chord, a sound Kansas City bands like Count Basie’s built whole arrangements on. Players bend into the “blue” notes between major and minor, answer each other in call and response, and take turns soloing chorus after chorus.
listen: Count Basie Orchestra, “One O’Clock Jump” (1937), a riff-built blues
Bessie Smith with Louis Armstrong, “St. Louis Blues” (1925)
liner.try: Use Trade fours: answer the riff with your own four bars. Write a three-line AAB lyric about your day and sing it over the band.

tunes.about: Handy wrote it in 1914 with three distinct strains; this is the famous 12-bar chorus in G. The flattened “blue notes” on B♭ give it its unmistakable character.
tunes.source: Melody transcribed from the original 1914 Pace & Handy Music Co. sheet music (chorus strain, 2/4 notated in 4/4); public domain. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: W. C. Handy, later called “the Father of the Blues,” published it in Memphis in 1914 through his own company, Pace & Handy. He said it was inspired by a woman he heard in St. Louis singing about the man who had left her. Handy built it from three strains, including a minor section in a tango (habanera) rhythm, mixing blues with the Latin dance rhythms popular at the time.
liner.tradition: It became one of the most recorded songs of the first half of the twentieth century. Bessie Smith’s 1925 version with Louis Armstrong’s cornet answering her lines is the model for blues singing with an instrument: call and response. Bands play the 12-bar strain in a loose two-beat swing, lean on the blue notes, and often slip into the tango rhythm for the minor section, which is not included in this lead sheet.

tunes.about: A 16-bar chorus that became one of the foundational jam-session tunes in early jazz (and the harmonic source for Miles Davis’s “Donna Lee”). Starts with a short pickup before bar 1.
tunes.source: Melody transcribed from the original 1917 Shapiro, Bernstein & Co. sheet music; public domain. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: James F. Hanley wrote the music and Ballard MacDonald the words in 1917, a sentimental song about going home to Indiana. The Original Dixieland Jass Band recorded it the same year, among the very first jazz records, and it became a jam-session standard. Since 1946 it has been sung before the start of the Indianapolis 500 motor race; Jim Nabors sang it there most years from 1972 to 2014.
liner.tradition: Dixieland and swing bands play it fast, often opening a set with it: Louis Armstrong’s All Stars used it as their theme. Bebop musicians kept the chords and wrote new melodies over them, a practice called a contrafact. “Donna Lee” (1947), recorded by Charlie Parker, is the famous example; Miles Davis said he wrote it. Players treat the chords as a racetrack for improvising long lines of eighth notes.
listen: Original Dixieland Jass Band (1917)
Louis Armstrong and His All Stars
Charlie Parker, “Donna Lee” (1947), new melody over the same chords
liner.try: Turn the melody off (Band only) and make up a new tune over the chords. That is how “Donna Lee” was born.

tunes.about: A 20-bar chorus instead of the usual 32: it starts away from home on the IV chord (E♭) and borrows its minor (E♭m6) on the way back to B♭, a move players still call the “After You’ve Gone” sound. A Dixieland and swing jam favorite, recorded by Bessie Smith, Louis Armstrong and Benny Goodman.
tunes.source: Melody from the concert lead sheet by the New Orleans Jazz Museum’s Public Domain Project (prepared by Evan Christopher), based on the original 1918 published sheet music; public domain. Common-practice chords. Chorus only; the verse is not included.

liner.origins: Turner Layton (music) and Henry Creamer (words) were an African American songwriting team in New York. Their song was a hit for the singer Marion Harris in 1918. Layton later moved to London and became a star in the piano-and-voice duo Layton & Johnstone. The lyric warns a lover that they will regret leaving.
liner.tradition: Singers often begin with the verse, sung freely out of tempo, then the band kicks into the chorus. Bessie Smith (1927) sang it as a blues; Louis Armstrong (1929) and the Benny Goodman Trio (1935) turned it into a fast showcase, with drum breaks and chorus after chorus of improvising. Judy Garland sang it in the film For Me and My Gal (1942). In Dixieland jams it is a tempo test: how fast can the band go and still swing?
listen: Marion Harris (1918)
Bessie Smith (1927)
Louis Armstrong (1929)
Benny Goodman Trio (1935)
liner.try: Start at 120 BPM, then raise the tempo by 8 BPM each chorus. Listen for the E♭ to E♭m6 move, the heart of the tune.

lyrics.credit: Words by Henry Creamer (1918, public domain)

tunes.about: A classic 32-bar AABA standard recorded by Miles Davis, John Coltrane, and countless others. The repeated quarter-note motifs make it ideal for practicing phrasing.
tunes.source: Melody transcribed from the original 1926 Jerome H. Remick & Co. sheet music; public domain. Chords adapted for this page.

liner.origins: Ray Henderson (music) and Mort Dixon (words) wrote it in 1926, a cheerful song about leaving troubles behind and heading home. Gene Austin’s recording that year was a big hit, and it stayed in the repertoire of dance bands and singers through the 1930s.
liner.tradition: Jazz musicians remade it in the 1950s. Miles Davis played it at a relaxed medium tempo on ’Round About Midnight (1957), using a Harmon mute and leaving lots of space between phrases; John Coltrane followed with long, dense lines. That contrast, few notes against many, is still how players learn it. Singers often slow it down and change the rhythm of each phrase.
listen: Gene Austin (1926)
Miles Davis, ’Round About Midnight (1957)
John Coltrane, Bye Bye Blackbird (live in Stockholm, 1962)
liner.try: Play the melody with long rests between phrases, as Miles did. Then try Push the beat and hear how much swing a few anticipations add.

tunes.about: Originally from the 1928 operetta The New Moon, this became an up-tempo jazz vehicle for Charlie Parker, Billie Holiday, and Dizzy Gillespie.
tunes.source: Melody transcribed from the original 1928 Harms Inc. sheet music; public domain. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: Sigmund Romberg (music) and Oscar Hammerstein II (words) wrote it for The New Moon (1928), an operetta set in eighteenth-century New Orleans. In the show it is a soaring romantic ballad. Its bridge closely follows a melody from Tchaikovsky’s piano piece “June” (Barcarolle) from The Seasons.
liner.tradition: Jazz musicians sped it up. Billie Holiday recorded it in 1944, and bebop players turned it into a fast vehicle for improvising. The A sections sit on long chords that leave room for running lines, while the minor bridge changes the mood. Many bands play the head at a racing tempo and drop the ballad feel completely.
listen: Billie Holiday (1944)
Tchaikovsky, The Seasons: “June” (to hear where the bridge comes from)
liner.try: Play it once with the Ballad band at a slow tempo, then with Swing at 200 BPM or faster. Same tune, two worlds.

lyrics.credit: Words by Oscar Hammerstein II, from The New Moon (1928, public domain)

tunes.about: Written as a tango for the 1928 operetta The New Moon, this minor-key standard became a staple of modern jazz (featured notably by Sonny Rollins and John Coltrane). Features quarter-note triplets in bars 16 and 18.
tunes.source: Melody transcribed from the original 1928 Harms Inc. sheet music (original 2/4 values doubled to 4/4); public domain. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: Another song from Romberg and Hammerstein’s The New Moon (1928). Despite the gentle title, in the show it is a cynical song about love: it starts as softly as a sunrise and can end in betrayal. It was written with a tango rhythm.
liner.tradition: Artie Shaw’s band swung it in 1938, but modern jazz made it a classic. The Modern Jazz Quartet, Sonny Rollins (A Night at the Village Vanguard, 1957) and John Coltrane (Live at the Village Vanguard, 1962) all recorded it. Bands often play a Latin or vamp feel on the minor A sections and swing the bridge, and use the minor ii–V chords as a playground for long solos.
listen: Artie Shaw (1938)
Sonny Rollins, A Night at the Village Vanguard (1957)
John Coltrane, Live at the Village Vanguard (1962)
liner.try: Switch the band between Bossa nova and Swing to hear the Latin-versus-swing contrast. Listen for the quarter-note triplets in bars 16 and 18.

lyrics.credit: Words by Oscar Hammerstein II, from The New Moon (1928, public domain)

tunes.about: Waller wrote this milestone 32-bar ballad for Connie’s Hot Chocolates in Harlem in 1929. The syncopated eighth-note figures swing naturally against the walking changes.
tunes.source: Melody transcribed from the original 1929 Mills Music Inc. sheet music; public domain. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: Fats Waller and Harry Brooks wrote the music and Andy Razaf the words for Connie’s Hot Chocolates (1929), a revue that started at Connie’s Inn in Harlem and moved to Broadway. A young Louis Armstrong played it from the orchestra pit during the show, and his 1929 recording made him a star with a wide audience. Waller recorded his own piano version the same year.
liner.tradition: Waller was a master of Harlem stride piano: the left hand leaps between a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 and a chord on beats 2 and 4, while the right hand plays the tune and fills. Singers deliver it with a wink, playing with the rhythm of the words. In 1978 a Broadway revue of Waller’s songs, Ain’t Misbehavin’, won the Tony Award for Best Musical.

Louis Armstrong (1929)
Ain’t Misbehavin’ (1978 Broadway cast)
liner.try: On piano, play the bass note on beats 1 and 3 and the chord on 2 and 4: that is the stride left hand. Use the Chords tab to find each shape.

tunes.about: Cole Porter’s masterpiece blends major and minor tonalities over a 32-bar form. Jazz musicians frequently play it at blistering tempos (and Tadd Dameron based “Hot House” on its chords). Features quarter-note triplets in the bridge.
tunes.source: Melody transcribed from the original 1929 Harms Inc. sheet music; public domain. Chords adapted for this page.

liner.origins: Cole Porter wrote it for the revue Wake Up and Dream, which opened in London and then on Broadway in 1929. Porter said the melody grew from music he heard in Marrakesh, Morocco. Each A section starts in a minor colour and resolves to major, which gives the tune its question-and-answer feeling.
liner.tradition: Jazz musicians love its chords: every A section is a chain of ii–V moves. In 1945 Tadd Dameron wrote a new bebop melody over them, “Hot House,” recorded by Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker. Clifford Brown and Max Roach played it at a blistering tempo. Bands often add a Latin feel to the A sections or start with a vamp.

Clifford Brown and Max Roach
liner.try: Use Matching scales on each chord to hear the minor-to-major shift. Then play Band only and improvise using only chord tones.

tunes.about: One of the defining swing themes in jazz history, composed by Fats Waller for the show Load of Coal. The A-section riff alternates over ii-V chords before landing on the tonic.
tunes.source: Melody transcribed from the original 1929 Santly Bros., Inc. sheet music; public domain. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: Fats Waller (music) and Andy Razaf (words) wrote it in 1929 for Load of Coal, a floor show at Connie’s Inn in Harlem. Waller’s own 1934 recording with his small band, Fats Waller and His Rhythm, made it a hit, full of his jokes and asides.
liner.tradition: Its riff-like A section, the same small phrase repeated over the two-chord ii–V, made it perfect for jam sessions and big bands. Count Basie’s band played it, and in Paris in 1937 Django Reinhardt recorded it with Coleman Hawkins and Benny Carter. Charlie Parker wrote “Scrapple from the Apple” over its A section chords. Musicians often answer the riff back and forth between sections of the band.

Coleman Hawkins and Django Reinhardt, Paris (1937)

tunes.about: Introduced by Ethel Merman in Girl Crazy, this song’s chord progression (“rhythm changes”) became the most played harmonic sequence in jazz after the 12-bar blues. Includes the original 2-bar tag ending (34 bars total).
tunes.source: Melody transcribed from the original 1930 New World Music Corp. sheet music (including the original 2-bar tag); public domain. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: George Gershwin (music) and Ira Gershwin (words) wrote it for the musical Girl Crazy (1930). Ethel Merman, in her Broadway debut, held a high note for sixteen bars and stopped the show. The pit band that night included future jazz stars Benny Goodman, Glenn Miller and Gene Krupa. Gershwin later wrote Variations on “I Got Rhythm” (1934) for piano and orchestra.
liner.tradition: Its chords, called “rhythm changes,” became the most played progression in jazz after the 12-bar blues. Musicians wrote hundreds of new tunes over them: “Anthropology,” “Oleo,” “Cotton Tail,” even the theme from The Flintstones. Players race through the A sections and then take the bridge’s chain of dominant chords (III7–VI7–II7–V7) as a challenge. Many players drop the two-bar tag that ends this original version.
listen: Ethel Merman (Girl Crazy, 1930)
Gershwin, Variations on “I Got Rhythm” (1934)
Sonny Rollins, “Oleo” (1954), new melody on rhythm changes

The 1930 composition is public domain in the United States; copyright terms differ elsewhere.

liner.origins: Hoagy Carmichael composed the music and Stuart Gorrell wrote the words. Southern Music published the song in New York in 1930. The title can sound like a person or a place, a useful question to bring to the first listening.
liner.tradition: The chorus has three related eight-bar A phrases around a contrasting bridge. Its slow, spacious melody invites singers and instrumentalists to stretch notes, while the chords move more quickly underneath. Ray Charles recorded a celebrated version in 1960; Georgia later designated the song its official state song.

tunes.about: A 32-bar AABA ballad. The A sections settle in D-flat; the bridge suddenly brightens to D major before a chromatic turnaround brings the final A home. The triplet on “body and” is written as three even notes in one beat.
tunes.source: Chorus melody transcribed from the 32-bar lead sheet at https://freedjazz.org/songs/body-and-soul/body-and-soul.pdf . The original 1930 Harms score is cataloged at https://imslp.org/wiki/Body_and_Soul_(Green,_Johnny). Chords simplified for this page; no lyrics or recording included. The 1930 composition entered the U.S. public domain in 2026; rights differ elsewhere.

liner.origins: Johnny Green wrote the music, and Edward Heyman, Robert Sour and Frank Eyton are credited for the words. The song appeared in the 1930 Broadway revue Three’s a Crowd. This chart presents the chorus, without the introductory verse.
liner.tradition: The spacious tune became a jazz ballad standard. Its bridge rises a semitone from D-flat to D major, then the last bridge bar leads back to E-flat minor for the final A. Players often reharmonize the A sections, so chord symbols can vary from chart to chart.
listen: Libby Holman, early vocal recording (1930)
Coleman Hawkins (1939), an improvised interpretation
liner.try: Play the melody alone and listen for the shift at bar 17. Then play the chords and follow the bass from D major through the bridge back to E-flat minor.

Each A bar pairs a minor chord with a dominant seventh a whole step below, then a major seventh with a dominant on its way home. The turnaround dominant is really F7♭9; this page plays it as F7.

liner.origins: Rollins wrote it for the 1966 film Alfie and recorded the score for Impulse! the same year. Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfie_(1966_film)
liner.tradition: Charts mark the A section “2 feel” (bass on beats 1 and 3) and the interlude “in 4” (walking), then “back to 2 feel” for the last A. The shift in feel is as much the form as the chords are.
listen: Sonny Rollins, Alfie (Impulse!, 1966)
liner.try: Loop bars 1–4 and name each chord’s job: minor home, dominant, major seventh, dominant. Then solo over the interlude using only D♭ and G♭ chord tones.

tunes.about: Chords only — no melody. Thirty-eight bars as played through: an eight-bar riff, a two-bar first ending, the riff again with a second ending, an eight-bar contrasting section, then the riff restated. The chart’s time signature is hard to read; this page uses 6/8. The chart sends soloists to a 12-bar blues in a different key, which is not included here.

liner.origins: Recorded by Mingus for Mingus Ah Um (Columbia, 1959). Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingus_Ah_Um
liner.tradition: The tune borrows the call-and-response of the church: a short shouted riff, an answer, and a held note that makes the band wait. Mingus asked his players to sound like a congregation, with clapping and shouts.
listen: Charles Mingus, Mingus Ah Um (Columbia, 1959)
liner.try: Play the riff on one note and answer it, congregation-style, in the two bars of rest.

liner.origins: Parker recorded it in New York for Savoy in November 1945, with Miles Davis and Dizzy Gillespie on the session. Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billie%27s_Bounce
liner.tradition: The blues in F is the beboppers’ common language: nearly every jam session starts with one. Learn the head’s changes, then solo over either chorus.
listen: Charlie Parker, Savoy sessions (1945)
liner.try: Loop bars 8–12 (the ii–V–I–VI–ii–V turnaround) until you can play it in every key.

tunes.source: Chord changes only, read from an E♭-instrument lead sheet and transposed to concert pitch for this page. No melody, lyrics or recording included; the lead sheet itself is not reproduced.

liner.origins: Written by Rodgers and Hart in the 1930s; the song became a hit in many versions. Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Moon_(1934_song)
liner.tradition: I–vi–ii–V is the engine of “rhythm changes” and of dozens of standards, and the same turnaround runs through this song’s A sections.
listen: The Marcels, “Blue Moon” (1961)
liner.try: Play only the root of each chord for the first A, then add the third, then the seventh.

tunes.about: A 32-bar form: A, a contrasting eight bars on B♭, A again, then a different last eight. The A section is a three-note pickup rising to a held note, answered by a descending line; the bridge climbs by half steps (C♯, D, then F) over B♭ major 7. The chords are transposed from the E♭-instrument lead sheet; Dm7–G7 turnarounds lead each section back.
tunes.source: Melody cross-checked note by note against the concert F lead sheet at https://gisementjazz.github.io/gisement/pdf/But%20not%20for%20me.C.pdf . Corrected the phrase peaks in bars 11 and 27 to F5 and bar 25 to F5. Repeats expanded to 32 bars; final note held through the practice ending. Existing simplified chords retained. Original 1930 edition: https://imslp.org/wiki/But_Not_for_Me_(Gershwin,_George) . No lyrics included.

liner.origins: Gershwin wrote it for the 1930 musical Girl Crazy; Ginger Rogers sang it in the original cast. Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/But_Not_for_Me_(song)
liner.tradition: A favorite of jazz players for its ii–Vs and its unexpected minor-subdominant turn. Miles Davis recorded it in 1956, and Ahmad Jamal’s 1958 live version is widely studied.
listen: Ahmad Jamal, At the Pershing: But Not for Me (1958)
Miles Davis Quintet, Workin’ (1956)

tunes.about: A 32-bar form with a rising four-note run as its signature: the same lick answers itself in the A sections, a bridge climbs a sixth in two stages, and the last A closes on a long held note. The lead sheet writes the song in cut time; it is notated here in 4/4. The augmented dominants (B+7) are played as plain D7, and the lead sheet’s second ending (a G with a half-rest, then a D7 and a final G) is not included.
tunes.source: Melody and chords transcribed by hand from a lead sheet for E♭ instruments (the Real Book), then transposed to concert pitch; pitches and rhythms are unchecked against a recording. The song (1930) is in the public domain.

liner.origins: Published in 1930 and made famous by Louis Armstrong’s 1930 recording. Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confessin%27_(That_I_Love_You)
liner.tradition: A relaxed two-beat swing, ideal for new improvisers: the changes are simple and the bridge makes a clear contrast.
listen: Louis Armstrong, “Confessin’” (1930)
liner.try: Play the bridge’s four chords as whole notes first, then improvise just on the bridge.

tunes.about: Chords only — no melody. A 32-bar form built on a chain of ii–V–I moves through the circle of fifths: Am7 Dm7 G7 Cmaj7, then Fmaj7 and a Dm6 (the same notes as Bm7♭5) into E7 and back to Am. Bars 10 and 26 pass quickly through Dm7 and back to G7. The last time through, the chart replaces bars 27–32 with an eight-bar closing ending: Cmaj7 | C7 | F6 | G7 | C6 | Am7 | Dm7 | C6.
tunes.source: Chord changes only, read from an E♭-instrument lead sheet and transposed to concert pitch for this page. No melody, lyrics or recording included; the lead sheet itself is not reproduced.

liner.origins: Bart Howard wrote it in 1954 as “In Other Words”; the opening line gave it the title people use today. Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fly_Me_to_the_Moon
liner.tradition: Players treat the chord chain as a drill in resolving fifths, and singers lean on the cycle to float the tune. It is usually played as a medium swing, though first recordings were waltz-time.
listen: Frank Sinatra with Count Basie, It Might as Well Be Swing (1964)
liner.try: Name each chord’s function as a Roman numeral, then notice that every dominant resolves down a fifth.

liner.origins: Schertzinger and Mercer wrote it for the 1942 film The Fleet’s In. Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Remember_You_(song)
liner.tradition: The passing chords in bars 2 and 6 (B m7 E7, then B♭m7 E♭7) give the tune its “borrowed-chord” colour. The last chart on the page credits Lee Konitz’s “Motion” as a reference recording.
listen: Lee Konitz, Motion (Verve, 1961)

liner.origins: Written by Van Heusen and Burke and recorded by many singers in the 1940s. Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It_Could_Happen_to_You_(song)

liner.origins: Written by Arthur Johnston with words by Johnny Burke for the 1936 Bing Crosby film Pennies from Heaven. Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennies_from_Heaven_(song)

tunes.about: A 32-bar chorus that starts away from home: four bars each of E7, A7 and D7 walk round the circle of fifths before the tune finally lands on G in bar 13. The second half repeats the walk, turns to E minor, and closes with a quick E7–A7–D7–G. Each melody phrase leans on the chord’s third (G♯ over E7, C♯ over A7, F♯ over D7), so you can hear the harmony in the tune alone.

tunes.about: A 32-bar chorus that opens on long whole notes (“Mar–gie”) and fills the gaps with stepwise pickups. Listen for the chromatic notes the tune leans on: B♮ against F (a diminished chord underneath), G♯ leading to A, C♯ leading to D. The written last bar is the first ending, which repeats the pickup; the second ending holds F.
tunes.source: Chorus melody transcribed from Margie, Mills Music, 1920 (a later reprint; IMSLP #697549), read from the voice line. Public domain. Chords read from the sheet’s guitar diagrams, with diminished chords named after the melody note they colour.

liner.origins: Con Conrad and J. Russel Robinson (the Original Dixieland Jazz Band’s pianist) wrote it in 1920, naming it after Eddie Cantor’s young daughter Marjorie. Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margie_(song)
liner.tradition: Cantor introduced it on stage; the Original Dixieland Jazz Band recorded it the same year. Dixieland bands still play it as a bright two-beat.

tunes.about: A 28-bar chorus as printed in 1922. It opens on D7, not the home chord, so the first phrase is already asking a question. The two “Stop!” bars (13 and 17) are stop-time breaks: the band hits one chord and drops out while the singer or a soloist fills. Bar 24’s E♭ over E♭7 is the surprise just before home.

Public domain. Chords read from the piano part and simplified. Later jazz versions often add bars and change the harmony.

liner.origins: Written by Henry Creamer and J. Turner Layton for the 1922 revue Strut Miss Lizzie; Creamer and Layton were a Black songwriting team who also wrote “After You’ve Gone.” Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Way_Down_Yonder_in_New_Orleans
liner.tradition: A Dixieland favourite. Bands use the breaks for short solo fills, and the last chorus is often collective improvisation.

tunes.about: A 32-bar AABA chorus. Each A climbs the C major scale (C, D, E, G) and leaps to a high E, then walks back down; the E♭ that follows is a blue note that bends the line toward the minor. The bridge settles on F and then reaches up through F♯ over D7. The chords here follow the piano part’s bass line and are simplified; jazz players often substitute ii–V pairs.

liner.origins: Jimmy McHugh and Dorothy Fields wrote it for Lew Leslie’s International Revue (1930); the song outlived the show. Fields was one of the first successful women lyricists on Broadway and Tin Pan Alley. Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Sunny_Side_of_the_Street
liner.tradition: A swing-era standard. Louis Armstrong recorded it in the 1930s, and Dizzy Gillespie with Sonny Stitt and Sonny Rollins made a famous 1957 version.

tunes.about: A 32-bar AABA refrain. The A sections rise from a low pentatonic phrase (B♭–C–E♭) step by step to the long held E♭; the bridge turns to G minor with the work calls, and the last A climbs to the song’s high point. The jazz changes are a later practice reharmonisation, not Kern’s accompaniment. The song’s Show Boat text depicts racism and the exploitation of Black laborers, so teach it with that context; no lyrics are included.
tunes.source: Refrain melody transcribed from Ol’ Man River, music by Jerome Kern, words by Oscar Hammerstein II, from Show Boat (T. B. Harms, 1927; IMSLP #835969), read from the voice line; where the climax is printed in two octaves, the upper is used. Composition public domain in the US since 2023. Chords: practice chart adapted from the iReal Pro jazz changes discussed at https://jazzchanges.app/ol-man-river/ .

liner.origins: Jerome Kern; words by Oscar Hammerstein II; 1927 · Show Boat. Background: https://imslp.org/wiki/Show_Boat_(Kern%2C_Jerome)
liner.tradition: Chords only — no melody. A 32-bar AABA jazz practice form in E-flat. The bridge moves toward G minor; performances and published arrangements use different changes. The song’s Show Boat text depicts racism and exploitation of Black laborers, so teach it with that context.
liner.try: Practice each eight-bar section separately. On the bridge, hear Gm7–D7 resolve before returning to E-flat; compare the jazz changes with the original theater score.

tunes.about: A slow minor blues about grief at a hospital morgue (“I went down to St. James Infirmary, saw my baby there”). Each verse is eight bars: the tune opens on a rising A–C–E minor arpeggio, and the harmony is just Am and E7 plus one chromatic color chord, F7, that slides down to E7 (F7 → E7 → Am). This chart plays the pattern twice, one chorus per verse. Jazz players usually take it in C minor; this lead sheet sits in A minor so it lies under the fingers on most instruments.
tunes.source: Traditional melody, notated here as a simplified practice arrangement from the widely sung folk tune (the song is a folk-blues with no single authoritative score). Chords simplified for this site; compare it with recordings and note where singers bend the melody.

liner.origins: The song grew out of an old British street ballad, “The Unfortunate Rake” (also “The Unfortunate Lad”), in which a dying soldier or young man is mourned by those he loved. In the United States the story moved to a hospital and a morgue, and the tune turned into a blues. Its authorship is unknown; Irving Mills published an arrangement in 1929–30 under the name Joe Primrose, but the song is much older than that credit.
liner.tradition: Sung and played slow, almost like a funeral march, with a steady four-beat pulse and plenty of space between the lines. A common arrangement starts with a vocal intro of Am – E7 – Am played twice, then sings verse after verse over the same eight bars, changing the words each time. Singers tell the story and bend the melody freely, so no two performances match.
listen: Louis Armstrong and His Savoy Ballroom Five (1928)
Cab Calloway in the Betty Boop cartoon Snow-White (1933)
Josh White’s acoustic folk-blues version
liner.try: Vamp Am – E7 – Am twice as the intro, then play the A–C–E pickup (“I went down”) on its own until it feels like a sigh. Listen for the F7 chord: it sits a half step above E7, and the slide F7 → E7 → Am is the song’s sad turn. Play the melody with Band only, bending a few notes the second time through.

tunes.about: The best-known Israeli hora: a bright circle-dance tune built on the Phrygian-dominant (“freygish”) scale. Here that is G minor with a D major chord under it, so the F♯ of the D chord sits against the E♭ of the minor key. The tune climbs through its verse, answers it, then lands on a repeated-note refrain that dancers shout.
tunes.source: Traditional melody, notated here as a simplified practice arrangement, following the commonly published melody and harmony. Rhythms and chords simplified for this site; compare with recordings.

liner.origins: The melody is a Hasidic nigun (wordless song) from Eastern Europe. Abraham Zvi Idelsohn, a cantor and musicologist in Jerusalem, set Hebrew words to it in 1918 to celebrate the British victory in Palestine; the words (“Let us rejoice”) are often credited to him, though students of the song disagree on how much was his work and how much his student Moshe Nathanson's. The tune's exact earlier history is not settled.
liner.tradition: Danced as a hora, a fast circle dance in which everyone holds hands and the circle speeds up. Klezmer bands play it with clarinet or violin leading, a steady oom-pah pulse underneath, and a faster tempo on each repeat. It is the standard dance at Jewish weddings and bar and bat mitzvahs.
listen: Any klezmer clarinet or violin recording — listen for how the player bends and slides into the notes
A school or wedding hora: notice the tempo creeping up each time through
liner.try: Play the melody slowly with Band only, then nudge the tempo up each time through, the way a hora speeds up. Find the E♭ to F♯ step: that augmented second is what gives the tune its flavor.

tunes.about: The complete 32-bar chorus in G, without the introductory verse. Quarter-note triplets gently stretch several phrases; the bridge moves into E-flat before returning to G. The final bar takes the closing ending.
tunes.source: Chorus vocal melody transcribed from the early piano-vocal sheet, printed pages 5–6: https://archive.org/details/dream-a-little-dream-of-me-sheet-music . This scan bears 1931; the composition was copyrighted in 1930 and entered the U.S. public domain in 2026: https://web.law.duke.edu/cspd/publicdomainday/2026/ . The underlying composition is public domain in the United States; terms differ elsewhere. Chords are a simplified practice harmonization for this page.

liner.origins: Fabian Andre and Wilbur Schwandt wrote the music, and Gus Kahn wrote the words. The song was copyrighted in 1930, with early recordings following in 1931.
liner.tradition: A relaxed vocal song that works as a ballad or gentle swing. The melody includes written triplets: let the words guide their shape rather than rushing them.

liner.origins: George and Ira Gershwin published the song in 1930 for Girl Crazy. This chart follows the chorus rather than the opening verse.
liner.tradition: A spacious ballad invites sustained tone and flexible phrasing. Practise with an even pulse first, then let the melodic phrases breathe while the accompaniment keeps time.
listen: Billie Holiday, Embraceable You (1944)
Charlie Parker, Embraceable You (1947)
liner.try: Loop bars 1–4 and count the opening rest aloud. Then follow the descending bass notes in bars 9–12.

liner.origins: Careless Love circulated as a traditional American song and became part of both folk and blues repertoires. Different performers use different words and melodic details.
liner.tradition: It can be sung with a steady country pulse or a slower blues feeling. This chart uses a 16-bar song form rather than assuming every blues song has twelve bars.
listen: Bessie Smith, Careless Love Blues (1925; a different lyric treatment)
liner.try: Count all sixteen bars while the band plays. Compare the major IV chord in bar 11 with the minor IV in bar 12.

liner.origins: An African American spiritual transmitted in more than one melodic and textual version. This chart identifies its particular traditional setting rather than treating one arrangement as the only version.
liner.tradition: The refrain and answering verse lend themselves to call and response. Sing the text to find the breath points; do not fill every rest with another note.
liner.try: Let one player take the refrain and another answer with the verse. Keep the quarter-note pickup at the end of bar 8 in time.

liner.origins: Ada R. Habershon wrote the words and Charles H. Gabriel composed the hymn in 1907. The later Carter Family song Can the Circle Be Unbroken reworked this material; this chart uses the earlier hymn.
liner.tradition: The dotted pickups give a gentle lift into the stronger beats. Keep verse and refrain distinct, and let the group breathe together at phrase endings.
liner.try: Sing the pickup on beat 4, then let the band enter on beat 1. Compare the verse in bars 1–8 with the refrain in bars 9–16.

liner.origins: Clarence Williams and Spencer Williams published Royal Garden Blues in 1919. The original score moves through several sections before reaching the vocal chorus used here.
liner.tradition: Early jazz ensembles trade short phrases between instruments. This chorus repeatedly names the instruments: use its rests for brief, coordinated answers rather than playing continuously.
liner.try: Take turns playing the two-bar figures. Keep each answer inside the written rests so the next phrase starts together.

liner.origins: Scott Joplin published The Entertainer with John Stark in 1902. This chart isolates its familiar first strain for melody-and-chord practice.
liner.tradition: Ragtime puts a syncopated melody over a steady accompaniment. Straight eighth notes and carefully sustained ties matter more than speed.
liner.try: Slow the band down and clap the melody before playing it. Hold tied notes across beats while the bass keeps an even pulse.

tunes.source: Traditional melody follows the Soldiers’ Joy entry in Colin Hume’s Eightsome Reel medley, mirrored at https://abcnotation.com/tunePage?a=colinhume.com/ABC.txt/1551 . liner.origins: Soldier’s Joy is a widely travelled traditional dance tune, shared by Scottish, Irish, English, and North American fiddle traditions. Melodic details vary by session.
liner.tradition: Play two A strains followed by two B strains. A light, steady dance pulse helps the arpeggios feel connected; speed can come later.
liner.try: Loop bars 1–8 slowly. Use small bow or pick movements, then listen for the higher register when the B strain starts at bar 17.

tunes.about: The traditional air in G, with the refrain and verse each repeated for 32 bars in 3/4. The verse ends in the relative minor; loop back to the refrain to hear the major-key return. This follows the older song, without later television lyrics or arrangements.

liner.origins: The traditional Scottish air was published with Sir Harold Boulton’s words in Songs of the North in 1884. The text recalls the escape to Skye after the 1746 Jacobite defeat.
liner.tradition: A gentle rowing motion suits the dotted phrases. The refrain is brighter, while the verse settles into the relative minor.
liner.try: Count three beats per bar and hold the tied notes for their full six beats. Compare the G-major refrain with the E-minor verse.

liner.tradition: A slow, even pulse gives singers room to shape each four-bar phrase.
liner.try: Take one breath at the end of each phrase. Then play the melody again and listen for the return to E-flat.

liner.tradition: The opening ascent sets up a broad, four-phrase melody.
liner.try: Play the opening E-flat chord as an arpeggio, then play bars 1 and 2 and identify the same pitches.

tunes.about: Written by Jelly Roll Morton around 1902 and published in 1925, uniting a twelve-bar blues with a ten-bar stomp chorus and four-bar coda.
tunes.source: Transcribed from the 1925 Melrose Bros. Music Co. edition (plate 573; public domain in the US); repeats written out with a chord reduction from the piano score.

liner.origins: Morton claimed to have composed “New Orleans Blues” around 1902 during his Gulf Coast travels; Melrose Bros. published the piano score in Chicago in 1925 after Morton’s 1923 solo recording.
liner.tradition: Notice how Morton pairs a relaxed twelve-bar blues with a bright ten-bar stomp strain — combining vocal blues phrasing with ragtime form.

tunes.about: Morton’s multi-strain stomp masterpiece in A♭ major, modulating to D♭ major at bar 57 for the Trio and building into the call-and-response Stomp and shout chorus.
tunes.source: Transcribed from the 1925 Melrose Bros. Music Co. edition (plate H.D.M.P. Co. 365; public domain in the US); repeats written out with top-line melody reduction and left-hand harmony.

liner.origins: Named after Florida pianist Porter King, whom Morton admired in the early 1900s. Morton recorded it in 1923–1924 and Melrose Bros. published the piano score in 1925.
liner.tradition: Its call-and-response Trio and Stomp strains became a blueprint for swing-era big-band arranging when Fletcher Henderson arranged it for Benny Goodman in 1935.
listen: Jelly Roll Morton (1923 / 1924 piano solos)
Benny Goodman and His Orchestra, arr. Fletcher Henderson (1935)
liner.try: Start at bar 57 (Trio) or bar 89 (Shout chorus) to practice the high call-and-response breaks against the stomping left-hand chord progression.

liner.tradition: Showcases Morton’s full ensemble conception: asymmetrical strain lengths (8, 16, 20, and 18 bars), stop-time two-bar solo breaks starting at bar 83, and a roaring final shout chorus.

tunes.about: Published in Chicago in 1915, uniting twelve-bar blues with Morton’s famous “Spanish tinge” habanera cross-rhythm at bar 53 and an E♭ Trio finale at bar 77.
tunes.source: Transcribed from the 1915 Will Rossiter edition (Chicago; public domain in the US); repeats and 1st/2nd endings written out cleanly.

liner.origins: Published by Will Rossiter in Chicago in 1915 as “The Jelly Roll Blues,” one of the first published jazz arrangements on paper.
liner.tradition: Morton demonstrated it at the Library of Congress in 1938 to explain the “Spanish tinge” — layering three-over-two habanera rhythms over New Orleans blues harmony.
listen: Jelly Roll Morton’s Red Hot Peppers (Victor, December 16, 1926)
Jelly Roll Morton (1938 Library of Congress piano solo)
liner.try: Jump to bar 53 to hear the Spanish-tinge habanera strain in isolation, then compare bar 5 with the B♭ blues turnaround.

tunes.about: Written for keyboard by Dresden organist Christian Petzold and copied into J. S. Bach’s 1725 notebook for Anna Magdalena. Notice how the A section climbs a five-note G-major scale before answering in parallel, while the B section touches D major before tumbling cleanly back to G.
tunes.source: Christian Petzold, Minuet in G major, BWV Anh. 114 (Notebook for Anna Magdalena Bach, c. 1720); public domain, verified against the flutetunes.com MIDI and engraving (mordents and repeat signs omitted for a straight 32-bar form).

liner.origins: For two centuries this beloved miniature was credited to J. S. Bach because it appeared in the 1725 music notebook assembled for his second wife, Anna Magdalena Bach. In the 1970s musicologist Hans-Joachim Schulze proved the two paired G-major/G-minor minuets were composed by Christian Petzold, organist at the Sophienkirche in Dresden.
liner.tradition: A Baroque minuet moves in steady three-beat dance groups (one-two-three, one-two-three), pairing balanced four-bar phrases with crisp counterpoint between melody and bass. Turning on Skeleton reveals the scalar framework underneath the eighth-note runs.
listen: Petzold, Minuet in G major, BWV Anh. 114 (harpsichord or piano)
The Toys, “A Lover’s Concerto” (1965), which turns Petzold’s 3/4 tune into 4/4 Motown pop
liner.try: Switch Chord tones on to trace every passing tone between chord notes, then push the tempo gently toward 120 BPM.

tunes.about: Brahms’s Wiegenlied uses only three chords (I, IV and V7) while rocking between the pickup eighth notes on beat 3 and warm, drooping thirds and sixths.
tunes.source: Johannes Brahms, Wiegenlied, Op. 49 No. 4 (1868); vocal melody verbatim from Mutopia 1037 (bars 3–19 after the two-bar piano intro, grace notes simplified), public domain.

liner.origins: Brahms wrote this song in 1868 for Bertha Faber, a young Viennese singer he had once been fond of, to celebrate the birth of her second son. In the piano accompaniment he wove a gentle cross-rhythm inspired by a Viennese folk waltz Bertha used to sing to him.
liner.tradition: Because every phrase begins on two eighth notes before the downbeat, the rhythm feels like a rocking cradle rather than a square march. Only two phrases answer each other before the whole tune climbs to Eb5 on the IV chord (Ab) and floats back home.
listen: Johannes Brahms, Wiegenlied, Op. 49 No. 4 (voice and piano in Eb major)
Cello or violin acoustic transcriptions (the entire melody stays inside a single octave!)
liner.try: Pay attention to how the harmony waits on Eb for the opening phrase, leans onto Bb7 for the answer, then blooms to Ab on the high Eb5.

tunes.about: The oboe’s weeping swan motif in B minor. After a two-bar harp ripple, the melody leaps a fifth down from F#5 to B4, climbs stepwise to high C#6 in the middle section, and drops unexpectedly into C major before returning home.
tunes.source: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, Swan Lake, Op. 20 (1876), Scene (No. 10) theme in B minor; transcribed verbatim from the CC0 Score Library piano arrangement.

liner.origins: Written for the Bolshoi Ballet premiere in 1877, this B-minor theme returns throughout Swan Lake as the signature motif of Odette and the enchanted swans. Over shivering string tremolos and harp arpeggios, a solo oboe sings the melody first.
liner.tradition: Watch bar 18 closely: after sequencing down A – F#m – Em, Tchaikovsky lands on C major (natural VI of E minor / Neapolitan color of B minor) instead of an expected minor chord, then pivots through C# and F# back to B minor.
listen: Tchaikovsky, Swan Lake, Op. 20, Act II Scene (No. 10, Moderato in B minor)
liner.try: Switch Chord tones on during bars 11–19 to watch the sequence step down from A major through F#m, Em and C major back to F#.

tunes.about: Written when Satie was twenty-one, this slow waltz floats back and forth between just two shimmering seventh chords (Gmaj7 and Dmaj7) before drifting through F-natural modal colors at the cadence.
tunes.source: Erik Satie, Gymnopédie No. 1 (1888), bars 1–39 (complete first half ending in D major); Mutopia 37 (Dover Edition), public domain.

liner.origins: Erik Satie published his Three Gymnopédies in Paris in 1888, naming them after ancient Spartan festivals of unadorned youth and slow ceremonial dance. Almost sixty years before ambient music got a name, Satie built an entire piece out of a hypnotic pendulum between IVmaj7 and Imaj7.
liner.tradition: In jazz and film harmony, Satie’s opening oscillation (Gmaj7 – Dmaj7) shows how major seventh chords suspend the pull toward a cadence. At bars 21 and 27 he drops F# to F-natural (Dm and Dm7), shading the sunlit D major briefly into D Dorian / D minor.
listen: Erik Satie, Trois Gymnopédies — No. 1 (piano, or Claude Debussy’s orchestration)
liner.try: Turn on Scale notes and watch bars 1–16 stay inside pure D major, then notice the unexpected F-naturals appear around bars 21–28.

tunes.about: Sixteen bars of Polish mazurka poise: a single dotted rhythm repeated eight times, climbing all the way to an unexpected bright F#7 chord at bar 12 before gently answering itself in A major.
tunes.source: Frédéric Chopin, Prelude in A major, Op. 28 No. 7 (1836–39); upper soprano voice extracted from Mutopia 470 (Edition Peters), public domain.

liner.origins: Chopin completed his 24 Preludes in Majorca during the stormy winter of 1838–39. No. 7 is the shortest of the set — just sixteen bars long — and pairs every two-bar question and answer on the same lilting dotted-eighth-to-sixteenth upbeat figure.
liner.tradition: For the first eleven bars the harmony moves calmly between E7 (V7) and A (I). In bar 12 Chopin suddenly brightens the melody onto a fortissimo F#7 chord (V7/ii), pulling the phrase cleanly through Bm and E7 to cadence at home.
listen: Frédéric Chopin, 24 Preludes, Op. 28 — No. 7 in A major (Andantino)
Watch for the harmonic color change at bar 12 on the F#7 climax
liner.try: Switch chord labels to Roman numerals and see how simple I–V7–I becomes dramatic solely because of that single V7/ii (F#7) detour in bar 12.

liner.origins: A minor blues swaps the major tonic dominant (I7) for minor seventh chords (Am7 and Dm7) and builds its dramatic turnaround around a half-diminished iiø7 (Bm7b5) resolving to E7.
liner.tradition: Compare bar 9–10 with major blues: instead of V7–IV7, jazz minor blues tunes (like John Coltrane’s “Equinox” or “Mr. P.C.”) love the bVI7 (F7) to V7 (E7) or iiø7–V7 cadence, letting soloists contrast the blues scale (A–C–D–Eb–E–G) with the raised leading tone G# on E7.
listen: John Coltrane, “Mr. P.C.” and “Equinox” (up-tempo and slow minor blues)
B.B. King, “The Thrill Is Gone” (minor blues in slow rock/soul feel)
liner.try: Use Trade fours or Mute melody on the empty even bars to improvise answers using A minor pentatonic plus Eb (the blue note).

tunes.source: Written for ClassroomOS; CC0 / free for any classroom to copy, perform and adapt.

liner.origins: In the late 1950s George Russell and Miles Davis moved away from fast-moving ii–V–I chords to let soloists explore a single scale for eight or sixteen bars at a time — stepping up one half step for contrast on the bridge.
liner.tradition: Dorian is just like natural minor except its sixth degree is raised a half step (B-natural instead of Bb in D minor). Rocking back and forth between im7 (Dm7) and iim7 (Em7) locks that bright B-natural right into the harmony.
listen: Miles Davis, “So What” (Kind of Blue, 1959 — D Dorian / Eb Dorian AABA)
liner.try: Switch on Scale notes, try improvising on the white keys alone over A, then shift everything up one fret or one piano key for the bridge.

liner.origins: Almost every standard from the 1930s through bebop stitches together major ii–V–I cadences (Dm7–G7–Cmaj7) and turnarounds (I–VI–ii–V) with brief detours to the relative minor (Bm7b5–E7–Am7).
liner.tradition: Voice leading is why great melodies outline the changes even without a chordal instrument: in bars 1–3, the 7th of Dm7 (C) becomes the 3rd of G7 (B), while the 3rd of Dm7 (F) stays put as the 7th of G7 before resolving to E on Cmaj7.
listen: Explore Skeleton mode and Chord tones together on this etude before improvising your own guide-tone lines
liner.try: Set Harmony mode to Skeleton so every bar highlights the 3rd and 7th resolution chain.

liner.tradition: Hundreds of pop, folk and rock hooks sit cleanly inside G major pentatonic (G–A–B–D–E) over both loops, touching F# mainly when D major passes through.

liner.origins: Introduced by Fred and Adele Astaire in the 1924 Broadway musical Lady, Be Good!, Fascinating Rhythm became an anthem of Jazz Age metric displacement. Notice how the chorus starts on the 9sus4 sound (Bb7sus4) instead of tonic Eb.
liner.tradition: Count the motif out loud in eighths: 1–2–3–4–5–6–(rest). Because the figure is seven eighths long inside an eight-eighth bar, each cycle lands earlier than the listener expects until it snaps onto Bb3 in bar 4.
listen: George Gershwin at the piano with Fred & Adele Astaire (1926 London recording)
Ella Fitzgerald, Ella Fitzgerald Sings the George and Ira Gershwin Songbook
liner.try: Clap beat 1 while singing or playing bars 1–4 straight (not swung) so you feel the seven-note cell rotating across the barline.

liner.origins: Composed for Gertrude Lawrence in the 1926 Broadway show Oh, Kay! — initially played as an uptempo rhythm number at George Gershwin’s own piano before Lee Wiley and Ella Fitzgerald made the tender slow tempo the norm.
liner.tradition: Watch bars 1–4 carefully: after the opening pentatonic arpeggio climbs Eb–F–G–Bb–C–Eb, the melody sighs downward in pairs while the left hand slips down chromatically step by step from Ab through F# and F to E7.
listen: George Gershwin solo piano recording (1926, Columbia)
Ella Fitzgerald with Ellis Larkins (Pure Ella, 1950)
liner.try: Switch Chord tones on during bars 2–4 to watch how each chromatic bass note reharmonizes the falling sigh.

tunes.about: Tárrega’s miniature masterpiece contrasts a sunlit eight-bar E-major opening against a shadowed E-minor middle section before returning home (A–B–A). Notice how just changing the third from G# to G-natural transforms the entire mood.
tunes.source: Francisco Tárrega, Lágrima (Madrid: Ildefonso Alier, plate 5230 A, IMSLP #292928); A–B–A upper voice and harmony transcribed from Mutopia 2103 (Public Domain) in concert octave.

liner.origins: Composed around 1891 and nicknamed “A Tear” (Lágrima), this sixteen-bar prelude (expanded here in its traditional 24-bar da capo A–B–A performance form) is one of the most recorded Romantic pieces for solo classical guitar.
liner.tradition: On classical guitar the upper voice sings over repeating open B-string bell tones in bars 1–4, then modulates to parallel E minor at bar 9 without changing a single finger of the rising G–A–B pattern—only lowering G# to G-natural.
listen: Francisco Tárrega, Lágrima (solo classical guitar in E major / E minor)
Compare the bright G# in bar 1 with the sorrowful G-natural in bar 13
liner.try: Switch to Guitar fingerboard view to watch how cleanly E major turns into parallel E minor at bar 9.
