liner.origins: Recorded in Paris in November 1937 by Django Reinhardt’s Quintette du Hot Club de France with violinist Stéphane Grappelli, Minor Swing has no long written theme—just an eight-bar signature opening motif and chorus after chorus over this taut sixteen-bar minor form.
liner.tradition: Because every chord lasts one or two full bars (with the rhythm guitar driving la pompe four-to-the-bar), Minor Swing is the doorway into Jazz Manouche improvisation: A minor arpeggios, A harmonic minor (for G# on E7), and bright Am6 (F#) colors.
listen: Django Reinhardt & Stéphane Grappelli, “Minor Swing” (1937 Paris recording)
liner.try: Solo using A minor pentatonic over Am6 and Dm6, then raise G to G# right on E7 in bars 5–6 and 14.

liner.origins: Recorded in occupied Paris in late 1940 with dual clarinets and acoustic guitars, Nuages (“Clouds”) became Reinhardt’s best-known ballad and an unofficial song of solace across wartime Europe.
liner.tradition: Instead of starting on a plain G tonic chord, Django opens bars 1 and 3 with chromatic backdoor/minor ii–V gestures (Gm7–C9 and Bbm7–Eb9) melting straight into Gmaj7, and answers in the coda with a classic IV–iv6 (C6–Cm6) sigh.
listen: Django Reinhardt et le Quintette du Hot Club de France, “Nuages” (1940)
liner.try: Switch on Skeleton mode and hear how C9 -> Gmaj7 and Eb9 -> Gmaj7 voice-lead smoothly around B and D.

liner.origins: Written during an intermission in Chicago and recorded in early 1932 with Ivie Anderson singing the refrain, this piece helped christen the Swing Era. Its bass line descends chromatically from G through F#, F and E down to Eb and D.
liner.tradition: Trace the inner voice across bars 1–5: G – F# (Gmmaj7) – F (Gm7) – E (C9) – Eb (Eb7) – D (D7). That descending chromatic inner line became one of the cornerstones of big-band arranging.

Ella Fitzgerald & Duke Ellington, Ella at Duke’s Place
liner.try: Use Scale notes or Skeleton on bars 1–5 to track the chromatic descent G -> F# -> F -> E -> Eb -> D.

liner.origins: Composed by Duke Ellington in 1935 (with lyrics later added by Manny Kurtz), this ballad became one of jazz’s signature saxophone showcases, memorably recorded by Ellington himself with John Coltrane in 1962.
liner.tradition: Ellington stacks two falling chromatic line clichés back to back in each A section (Dm–Dmmaj7–Dm7–G7 on i, then Gm–Gmmaj7–Gm7–C7 on iv), then brightens everything on the bridge by slipping down a half step to Dbmaj7.
listen: Duke Ellington & John Coltrane, “In a Sentimental Mood” (1962)
Ella Fitzgerald Sings the Duke Ellington Song Book (1957)
liner.try: Trace the guide-tone descent D -> C# -> C -> B across bars 1–4, then repeat the pattern down a fifth on G -> F# -> F -> E.

liner.origins: Written by Armstrong’s mentor Joe “King” Oliver (named for the Lake Pontchartrain resort outside New Orleans), West End Blues was transformed in June 1928 by Louis Armstrong’s unforgettable unaccompanied trumpet cadenza and vocal–clarinet call and response.
liner.tradition: Notice how this early New Orleans 12-bar blues enriches the IV chord in bars 5–6 (Ab7 -> Abdim7 -> Eb) and adds C7 in bar 8 to pull cleanly into the Fm7–Bb7 turnaround.
listen: Louis Armstrong and His Hot Five, “West End Blues” (Okeh, June 28, 1928)
liner.try: Leave lots of breathing space between short two-bar phrases—just like Armstrong’s 1928 solo—and lean into the Abdim7 passing chord at bar 6.

liner.origins: Written in Rio de Janeiro in 1962 and recorded worldwide in 1963–64 by João Gilberto, Stan Getz and Astrud Gilberto, Garota de Ipanema brought the hushed guitar-and-clave syncopation of bossa nova into global jazz repertoire.
liner.tradition: Study the bridge (bars 17–32): three four-bar dominant plateaus (Gbmaj7–B7, F#m7–D7, Gm7–Eb7) drift slowly downward like keys shifting by a half step until Am7–D7b9–Gm7–C7b9 snaps smoothly back into F major.
listen: Getz / Gilberto (1964), featuring João Gilberto, Stan Getz and Astrud Gilberto
liner.try: Switch Chord tones on across bars 17–24 to watch how Gb and B7 share half-step guide tones with F#m7 and D7.

liner.origins: Composed by guitarist Luiz Bonfá for Marcel Camus’s 1959 Rio film Orfeu Negro, Manhã de Carnaval became an essential early bossa standard for acoustic guitarists and horn players alike.
liner.tradition: Compare the two halves: bars 9–15 cycle through major ii–V–I (G7–Cmaj7–Fmaj7–Bm7b5–E7–Am7), while bars 21–24 tonicize the minor subdominant (Em7b5–A7–Dm7).

liner.origins: Named after the Rio mountain overlooking Guanabara Bay, Corcovado pairs whisper-soft acoustic rhythm with chromatic voice leading that seems to sigh downward measure by measure.
liner.tradition: In bars 1–8 the top inner voices slide down half steps against a gentle bass: F# (D7/A) -> F (Abdim7 / Gm7) -> E (C9 / Fmaj7) -> D/Ab (Fm6), resolving cleanly into Em7.
listen: João Gilberto & Antônio Carlos Jobim, “Corcovado” (1964)

liner.origins: Title track of Jobim’s landmark 1967 instrumental album recorded with Claus Ogerman’s studio orchestra, Wave stretches standard 8-bar sections to 12 bars so the chord sequence can wind effortlessly down the cycle of fifths.
liner.tradition: Notice how the bridge (bars 25–32) steps cleanly through two distant key centers in four bars apiece — Gm7–C7–Fmaj7 followed by Fm7–Bb7–Ebmaj7 — before A7 swings back to Dmaj7.
listen: Antônio Carlos Jobim, Wave (1967)

liner.origins: Introduced in 1937, the waltz was transformed into a flagship 3/4 modern-jazz vehicle during the late 1950s and early 1960s, famously anchored by a hypnotic F-pedal vamp in Miles Davis’s 1961 recording with John Coltrane.
liner.tradition: Watch the chromatic passing chords in bars 9–16 (Dm7–Dbm7–Cm7–F7 and Dm7–Dbdim7–Cm7–F7) and the classic IV–#iv°7–I/V climax in bars 27–29.

liner.origins: Written in the mid-1950s for his young niece Debby and forever associated with the Bill Evans Trio’s landmark 1961 Live at the Village Vanguard sessions with Scott LaFaro and Paul Motian, this piece taught generations of jazz musicians how fluidly a waltz could swing.
liner.tradition: Feel the one-bar-per-chord motion in larger two-bar and four-bar hypermeasures: I–vi–ii–V leading cleanly through iii–vi–ii–V and dominant turnaround chains.
listen: Bill Evans Trio, Waltz for Debby (Live at the Village Vanguard, 1961)
liner.try: Trace the cycle of dominants in bars 9–12 (A7 -> D7 -> G7 -> C7) using guide tones on piano or guitar.

liner.origins: Written in 1962 by Belgian jazz harmonica virtuoso and guitarist Jean “Toots” Thielemans (who famously whistled the unison melody with his own guitar!), Bluesette squeezed the harmonic motion of a swinging standard into a crisp 24-bar waltz cycle.
liner.tradition: Notice how clean the modulation map is: tonic Bbmaj7 steps via Am7–D7 to Gm7–C7, then Fm7–Bb7–Ebmaj7 shifts parallel minor (Ebm7–Ab7) down through Dbmaj7 and Gb7 back to Cm7–F7–Bbmaj7.
listen: Toots Thielemans, “Bluesette” (1962 recording, whistled melody & guitar)
liner.try: Keep Roman numerals off at first and practice spotting each new key’s ii–V pair on sight (Am7–D7, Gm7–C7, Fm7–Bb7, Ebm7–Ab7).

tunes.about: One of the first tunes learned at every Irish traditional session: a buoyant G-major 6/8 double jig that moves effortlessly between the G chord and its D7 answer in eight-bar A and B halves.
tunes.source: Traditional Irish double jig (19th c., public domain); single A+B chorus verified from flutetunes.com #774 (repeats omitted).

liner.origins: Named for Kesh, a village in County Sligo, The Kesh Jig has become one of the universal session openers from Doolin to Boston because its phrases sing effortlessly on whistle, flute, fiddle, accordion and guitar.
liner.tradition: In a 6/8 double jig you feel two big dotted-quarter beats per bar (“ONE-two-three FOUR-five-six”), not six stiff taps. Players often double each part (AA BB) and link it straight into another G-major jig in a medley.
listen: Search Irish session recordings of The Kesh Jig (often paired with Morrison’s Jig or Out on the Ocean)
liner.try: Switch to Violin or Guitar fingerboard view at 95 BPM first, then gradually push up to session speed (120 BPM).

tunes.about: A driving E-Dorian (two-sharp minor with C# natural sixth) Irish double jig popularized by Sligo fiddler James Morrison. Notice how flipping between Em and D chords captures that unmistakable modal lift.

liner.origins: Named after County Sligo fiddler James Morrison, this E-Dorian double jig is a staple of Irish traditional sessions worldwide and often closes sets paired with The Kesh Jig.
liner.tradition: Because E Dorian uses F# and C# (the notes of D major centered on E), backing instruments rock back and forth between Em (i) and D (bVII) rather than using B7.
listen: Search Irish session recordings of Morrison’s Jig paired with The Kesh Jig or Drowsy Maggie

tunes.about: Published in 1863 in sweeping 6/8 minor time, setting natural minor (F natural in bars 3–4) alongside a sharp raised leading tone (F# in bar 15) as the march drives home to G minor.
tunes.source: Patrick Gilmore, When Johnny Comes Marching Home (1863, G minor); verified from flutetunes.com #15, public domain.

liner.origins: Boston bandleader Patrick S. Gilmore published the song in September 1863 during the American Civil War, adapting an older Irish anti-war song cadence (“Johnny I Hardly Knew Ye”) into a driving 6/8 march.
liner.tradition: Musically the tune pivots smoothly between G natural minor (dropping cleanly onto F major in bars 3–4 and Bb major in bar 7) and G harmonic minor right at the end, where F# on D7 snaps back to G.
listen: Morton Gould, American Salute (orchestral variations built entirely on this 16-bar tune)
liner.try: Watch bar 15 with Scale notes enabled: F-natural rules bars 3–13, then F# sharpens cleanly on the D7 cadence.

tunes.source: Gabriel Fauré, Pavane, Op. 50 (1887), opening theme bars 1–17 in F# minor; verified against flutetunes.com #189 & #692 MIDI and engraving, public domain.

liner.origins: Composed in 1887 as an orchestral salon work (and later given an optional invisible chorus), Fauré’s Pavane opens with a quiet solo flute tracing a stately 16th-century court dance over gently plucked strings.
liner.tradition: Listen to the bass line under the first eight bars: F# – D – E – C# – D – B – C# – B – A – F# – B – E – A – G# – C#. Almost every bar re-harmonizes a falling sequence of sevenths without ever sounding heavy.

tunes.title: Come, Ye Thankful People, Come
tunes.composer: George J. Elvey · words by Henry Alford

tunes.about: The classic English and American harvest-festival and Thanksgiving processional hymn (tune St. George’s Windsor, 1858). Notice how bar 4 surprises gently on A7 (leading to Dm), bar 8 cadences cleanly into C major (V), and bar 13 touches D7 on the final climb home.
tunes.source: George J. Elvey, St. George’s Windsor (1858); words by Henry Alford (1844); melody and 4-part harmony verified against the full SATB LilyPond setting, public domain.

liner.origins: English dean and hymn-writer Henry Alford wrote the harvest lyrics in 1844, and Sir George Job Elvey — organist of St. George’s Chapel, Windsor Castle — composed this sturdy F-major tune in 1858.
liner.tradition: Sung at parish harvest festivals across Britain and at Thanksgiving services in North America, its clean dotted-quarter march rhythm teaches secondary dominants naturally: A7 turns toward D minor in bar 4, G7 moves to C in bar 8, and D7 lifts into G minor at bar 13.
listen: St. George’s Windsor sung in four-part choir and organ
Try Skeleton mode to trace the I–V/V–V modulation at bar 8

liner.origins: Country harvest-supper airs like Harvest Time paired easy, singable A-major phrases with nimble 6/8 stepping figures for fiddles, flutes and concertinas.
liner.tradition: Notice bar 15: the brief D# on “B7” lights up the middle B section by modulating smoothly onto E7 (V) before gliding back to the A-major refrain at bar 17.

tunes.about: Vivaldi’s joyful opening harvest-celebration ritornello from L’Autunno (“Autumn”), alternating bold upper-octave statements with quiet lower-octave echoes over a sturdy F–Bb–C7 dance progression.
tunes.source: Antonio Vivaldi, Concerto in F major “L’Autunno”, Op. 8 No. 3, RV 293 (c. 1723), bars 1–11 opening ritornello; verified against flutetunes.com #620 MIDI and engraving, public domain.

liner.origins: Vivaldi printed a sonnet alongside The Four Seasons explaining each concerto; Autumn opens with the line “Celebrates the peasant, with songs and dances, the joy of a fine harvest.”
liner.tradition: Compare bars 1–3 with bars 4–6: Vivaldi repeats the exact phrase an octave lower (terraced dynamics—forte then piano) before climbing cleanly through Bb (IV) and C7 (V7) in bars 7–11.
listen: Antonio Vivaldi, Le quattro stagioni — L’Autunno (I. Allegro)
liner.try: Switch to Guitar or Violin view to see how the exact same F-major harvest riff sits one octave apart between bars 1–3 and bars 4–6.

tunes.about: Written in Mexico in 1882 by Quirino Mendoza y Cortés, this bright C-major waltz floats ties smoothly across barlines before bursting into the soaring “Ay, ay, ay, ay!” chorus at bar 17.
tunes.source: Quirino Mendoza y Cortés, Cielito Lindo (1882); verified against flutetunes.com #430 MIDI and engraving, public domain.

liner.origins: Composed around 1882 in Xochimilco, Mexico City, by Quirino Mendoza y Cortés, Cielito Lindo became one of Mexico’s defining cultural songs and a standard of mariachi repertoire around the world.
liner.tradition: Feel how each phrase ties beat 3 over into beat 1 of the next bar (forming a gentle cross-rhythm hemiola across the fast one-in-a-bar waltz pulse) before the chorus opens wide on sustained dotted halves at bar 17.
listen: Mariachi Vargas de Tecalitlán, “Cielito Lindo” (listen for the vihuela and guitarrón 3/4 groove)
liner.try: Trace how bars 1–16 stay on C and G7–Dm before the chorus lifts immediately through C7 into F (IV) at bar 19.

tunes.title: Arirang
tunes.melody: D4q. E4e D4e E4e | G4q. A4e G4e A4e | B4q A4e B4e G4e E4e | D4q. E4e D4e E4e | G4q. A4e G4e A4e | B4q. A4e D4e E4e | G4q. A4e G4q | G4h rq | D5h D5q | D5q B4q A4q | D5q B4e A4e G4e E4e | D4h rq | G4q. G4e G4e A4e | B4q. A4e D4e E4e | G4q. A4e G4q | G4h rq
tunes.about: Korea’s most iconic folk melody, flowing in a gentle three-beat semachi lilt using purely the five-note major pentatonic scale (G–A–B–D–E) without a single F# or C!
tunes.source: Traditional Korean folk song (public domain); verified against flutetunes.com #305 MIDI and engraving (placed in G4/D4 octave for singability).

liner.origins: Sung across the Korean peninsula for centuries (and twice inscribed by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage), the Gyeonggi Arirang version popularized in the late 19th and early 20th centuries is built in sixteen symmetrical bars.
liner.tradition: Turn Scale notes or Chord tones on and notice what is missing: out of all sixteen bars, the melody uses ONLY five notes—G, A, B, D and E (no C and no F#)—yielding that unmistakable open pentatonic beauty.
listen: Traditional Gyeonggi Arirang (gayageum, daegeum, or vocal performance in 3/4 semachi rhythm)
liner.try: Switch Harmony off or Mute chords and hear how complete the five-note G–A–B–D–E scale sounds all by itself.

tunes.about: The beloved Mexican birthday serenade (“Estas son las mañanitas…”) in warm G-major 3/4 time: two clear eight-bar halves moving gently between I, IV and V7.
tunes.source: Traditional Mexican (19th century, public domain); verified against flutetunes.com #419 MIDI and engraving.

liner.origins: Sung outdoors at dawn to celebrate birthdays, Mother’s Day and saint’s days across Mexico and Latin America, Las Mañanitas opens with an affectionate 3/4 verse before brightening in bar 9 (“Despierta, mi bien, despierta”).
liner.tradition: Every phrase leans cleanly on the three primary chords of G major — G (I), C (IV) and D7 (V7) — making it an ideal waltz for beginner chord-by-ear harmony.
listen: Pedro Infante or mariachi recordings of “Las Mañanitas”
liner.try: Notice how bars 9–12 echo the exact same call-and-answer D7 -> G harmonic oscillation twice before C arrives at bar 13.

tunes.about: One of the world’s best-known traditional Chinese melodies, dating back to the 18th-century Qianlong era. All sixteen bars move strictly through the five pentatonic tones G–A–B–D–E without any half steps.
tunes.source: Traditional Chinese folk song (18th century, public domain); verified against flutetunes.com #713 MIDI and engraving.

liner.origins: First printed in Chinese songbooks during the 1790s and brought to Western readers in 1804 by John Barrow’s Travels in China, Mo Li Hua later inspired Puccini’s Turandot.
liner.tradition: Like Arirang, this Jiangnan folk melody stays strictly inside the five-note Gong pentatonic collection (G–A–B–D–E). Even as the harmony shifts underneath between G, Em, C and D chords, the melody never needs F# or C.
listen: Traditional guzheng, erhu or bamboo dizi performances of Mo Li Hua
liner.try: Play along improvisationally using only G–A–B–D–E on your instrument—none of those five notes clash anywhere in the sixteen bars.

tunes.about: Puerto Rico’s beloved danza national anthem, contrasting a yearning G-minor opening (driven by the cinquillo/habanera sixteenth turn in bar 1) with a radiant parallel G-major middle section before slipping back to G minor at the coda.
tunes.source: Félix Astol Artés, La Borinqueña (1867); verified against flutetunes.com #237 MIDI and engraving, public domain.

liner.origins: Composed as a romantic Puerto Rican danza by Félix Astol Artés in 1867 (and soon given revolutionary lyrics by Lola Rodríguez de Tió and later official civic lyrics by Manuel Fernández Juncos), La Borinqueña showcases the graceful Afro-Caribbean danza rhythm.
liner.tradition: Like Tárrega’s Lágrima and classic ragtime-era dances, the form pivots directly between parallel minor and major on the same tonic note G: brooding G minor in bars 1–12, sunlit G major at bar 13, then a minor cadence at bars 19–22.
listen: Traditional Puerto Rican danza piano or orchestra recordings of La Borinqueña
liner.try: Watch bar 13 carefully: turning from Bb to B-natural brightens the entire band texture without leaving tonic G.

tunes.about: Two chords carry the whole song: G and D7. Each phrase starts with three quick pickup notes (“la cu-ca-”) that tumble into a long note on the beat, then a tied note that lands just before beat 3.
tunes.source: Traditional, public domain. Melody from the flutetunes.com setting (https://www.flutetunes.com/tunes.php?id=228), MIDI and engraving, with the repeats written out. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: La Cucaracha (“the cockroach”) is a Spanish-language folk song whose tune and verses are much older than any one printing; versions were sung in Spain and Mexico in the 19th century. It became famous during the Mexican Revolution (1910–1920), when soldiers on different sides made up new verses about their leaders and their hardships.
liner.tradition: Singers have always invented their own verses, so there is no single set of words. The chorus usually comes first and is played by mariachi and brass bands with a bright two-beat bass.
listen: Any mariachi recording of “La Cucaracha” (listen for the guitarrón playing root and fifth)
liner.try: Clap the three pickup eighth notes, then hold. Count “1-and-2-and” out loud through bar 1 and feel the tied B land on the “and” of 2.

tunes.about: A verse of long, held notes that climbs in steps (G, then D, then F), then the famous chorus: two short shouts (“Jammo, jammo!”) and a run of repeated Gs for “funiculì, funiculà.”
tunes.source: Luigi Denza, Funiculì, Funiculà (1880), public domain. Melody from the flutetunes.com setting (https://www.flutetunes.com/tunes.php?id=333), MIDI and engraving, written an octave lower for singing and with the chorus taken once. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: Written in Naples in 1880 by the journalist Peppino Turco and the composer Luigi Denza for the opening of the funicular railway that carried visitors up Mount Vesuvius. It was an instant hit across Europe. Richard Strauss used the tune in his 1886 symphonic fantasy Aus Italien, apparently thinking it was a folk song; Denza is reported to have sued and won a share of the royalties.
liner.tradition: A Neapolitan canzone sung by tenors and street bands alike, usually with a mandolin and guitar keeping the six-eight lilt. The chorus gets faster and louder each time round.
listen: Any tenor recording with orchestra (Luciano Pavarotti’s is well known)
Neapolitan mandolin-and-guitar versions
liner.try: Feel two big beats in each bar (ONE-and-a TWO-and-a). In the chorus, hit the short notes on beat one and leave the rest of the bar silent, like a shout.

tunes.about: The chorus repeats one three-note cell (D–B–C) over and over, falling to A at the end of each phrase. The verse slows into long whole notes in C major before the chorus returns in A minor.
tunes.source: Ivan Larionov, Kalinka (1860), public domain. Melody from the flutetunes.com setting (https://www.flutetunes.com/tunes.php?id=798), MIDI and engraving. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: Kalinka was written in 1860 by the composer and folklorist Ivan Larionov for a theatre show in Saratov, in a folk style so convincing that many people think it is a traditional song. “Kalinka” means a little snowball-tree berry (guelder rose), and “malinka” a little raspberry.
liner.tradition: Russian ensembles and choirs usually start the chorus slowly and speed up every time it comes round, until the dancers can barely keep up. The verse is sung slowly and freely in between.
listen: The Red Army Choir (Alexandrov Ensemble), “Kalinka”
liner.try: Loop the chorus and raise the tempo a little each time, the way a Russian ensemble does. Notice how the same D–B–C cell sounds more exciting the faster it goes.

tunes.melody: C5e C5e C5q D5e D5e D5q | E5e F5e G5e C5e B4e C5e D5e G4e | C5e C5e C5q D5e D5e D5q | E5e F5e G5e C5e D5e B4e C5q | C5e C5s C5s C5e C5e D5q C5q | C5e. tunes.about: Three notes up (C–D–E) and back down, over just C and G: one of the simplest songs in the book. The middle verse sits on one repeated note while the words describe a dance step.
tunes.source: Traditional French song, public domain. Melody from the flutetunes.com setting (https://www.flutetunes.com/tunes.php?id=856), MIDI and engraving, rebarred from 2/4 into 4/4. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: The song is about the Pont Saint-Bénézet, a 12th-century bridge across the Rhône at Avignon whose arches were washed away by floods until only four remained. Its tune is old; it became widely known after Adolphe Adam used it in his comic opera Le Sourd, ou l’Auberge pleine in 1853. People probably danced under the bridge (“sous le pont”) on the island it crossed, rather than on the narrow bridge itself.
liner.tradition: A circle-dance song: children sing the chorus while dancing round, then stop and act out each verse (“les beaux messieurs font comm’ ça”) with a bow, a curtsy or a salute.
listen: Any French children’s choir recording
liner.try: Sing the chorus, then make up your own verse for bars 5–6: who else could be on the bridge, and what move do they make?

tunes.about: A slow farewell song built on three chords (Ab, Db and Eb7). The chorus opens with a leap up to a long Db, the note that makes “Aloha ʻoe” sound so tender.
tunes.source: Liliʻuokalani, Aloha ʻOe (1878), public domain. Melody from the flutetunes.com setting (https://www.flutetunes.com/tunes.php?id=349), MIDI and engraving; chords follow that setting’s piano accompaniment.

liner.origins: Written in 1878 by Liliʻuokalani, later the last reigning monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom. The story usually told is that she wrote it after watching a fond goodbye between two people at the end of a horseback ride near Maunawili on Oʻahu. “Aloha ʻoe” means “farewell to you.”
liner.tradition: It is sung at partings of every kind in Hawaiʻi, often with ukulele, steel guitar and slow, rolling chords. Liliʻuokalani was a trained musician who wrote more than 150 songs.
listen: Recordings by Hawaiian steel-guitar players and slack-key guitarists
Choral performances in Hawaiian
liner.try: Play it slowly with Harmony on and listen for the Eb7 in bars 3–4 and 11: it pulls you back home to Ab every time.

liner.origins: The poet A. B. “Banjo” Paterson wrote the words in 1895 at Dagworth Station in Queensland, to a tune Christina Macpherson played from memory, probably based on a Scottish march. In 1903 Marie Cowan rearranged it for a tea company’s advertisement, and her version is the one sung today. It tells of a swagman (a wandering worker) who steals a sheep.
liner.tradition: Often called Australia’s unofficial national anthem, it is sung at sporting events and by Australian soldiers. “Waltzing Matilda” is slang for walking the roads with your swag, your bundle of belongings.
listen: Any Australian folk recording
Massed crowd singing at a rugby or cricket match
liner.try: Try the dotted rhythm two ways: straight and with Swing on. Which sounds more like someone marching along a dusty road?

liner.origins: The tune, the “Londonderry Air,” was noted down by Jane Ross of Limavady in County Londonderry and published by George Petrie in The Ancient Music of Ireland in 1855, with no words. The English songwriter Frederic Weatherly wrote “Danny Boy” in 1910 and fitted it to the air in 1913.
liner.tradition: It is sung slowly and freely, often at funerals and farewells, and played on uilleann pipes, fiddle and brass. Singers stretch the high notes in bar 13 and let the last phrase fade.
listen: Any slow air on uilleann pipes or fiddle
Classic vocal recordings by Irish tenors

tunes.about: A gentle waltz where almost every bar has the same rhythm: an eighth note, then a dotted quarter that lands just after the beat. That little lilt is what makes it sound like a street cry.
tunes.source: Public domain. Melody from the flutetunes.com setting (https://www.flutetunes.com/tunes.php?id=235), MIDI and engraving. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: The song first appears in print in the early 1880s, in a student songbook in Cambridge, Massachusetts and in an Edinburgh edition credited to James Yorkston. It tells of a Dublin fishmonger who sells cockles and mussels from a wheelbarrow and dies young of a fever.
liner.tradition: It has become Dublin’s unofficial anthem, sung by sports fans and in pubs. There was probably no real Molly Malone, but a statue of her with her barrow stands on Suffolk Street in Dublin.
listen: Recordings by Irish folk groups such as The Dubliners
liner.try: Count “1-and-2-and-3” and clap only the notes. Bars 2, 4, 10 and 12 all use the same short-long rhythm.

liner.origins: “The Bonnie Banks o’ Loch Lomond” was first published in 1841 in Vocal Melodies of Scotland. A popular explanation, impossible to prove, is that it is sung by a Jacobite prisoner after 1746: “the low road” is the road the dead take home to Scotland, faster than the living friend on “the high road.”
liner.tradition: Sung slowly by soloists and fast by ceilidh bands and pipe bands; crowds sing the chorus together at the end of Scottish dances.
listen: Any Scottish pipe-band arrangement
Choral versions that start slow and finish fast
liner.try: Play it once as a slow ballad, then switch the band to Two-beat at a faster tempo, the way a ceilidh band would.

liner.origins: A work song from the days of sailing ships, sung while hauling on ropes or walking round the capstan. It was described in sailors’ accounts in the 19th century and later collected by shanty collectors such as Cecil Sharp and Stan Hugill.
liner.tradition: A leader (the shantyman) sings the question and the crew roars back the answer, pulling on the strong beats. Crews made up endless new verses about what to do with the drunken sailor.
listen: Any shanty choir or folk recording
liner.try: Turn on Scale notes and find the B natural. That one note is what makes the Dorian mode sound brighter than ordinary minor.

liner.origins: Brewster Higley, a doctor living in a cabin in Smith County, Kansas, wrote the poem around 1872, and his neighbour Daniel Kelley set it to music. Cowboys carried it across the West, and the folklorist John Lomax printed it in 1910. Kansas made it the state song in 1947.
liner.tradition: Sung slowly by cowboy singers with a guitar in a gentle three, often with harmony in the chorus.
listen: Early cowboy-song recordings and campfire-style versions

liner.origins: Nobody knows who wrote it. Some trace it to the Red River of the North in Manitoba around the time of the 1870 Red River Rebellion; a version called “In the Bright Mohawk Valley” was published in New York in 1896. Either way, it is a song about someone leaving and being missed.
liner.tradition: A cowboy and country standard, sung slowly with guitar and played on harmonica and fiddle.
listen: Early country and cowboy recordings
liner.try: Sing the pickup “From this” softly and lean on the first beat of each bar.

lyrics.credit: Traditional words (public domain)

liner.origins: Its roots are uncertain. It may have started with river boatmen or fur traders on the Missouri; Shenandoah is the name of a river in Virginia and of an Oneida chief. Sailors took it to sea as a capstan shanty, and it was in print by the 1880s.
liner.tradition: Sung slowly and freely, by soloists, choirs and sailors, with plenty of time on the held notes.
listen: Choral arrangements
Solo folk recordings with guitar or unaccompanied
liner.try: Play it at a slow tempo and hold each tied note its full length before moving on.

liner.origins: Jack Norworth wrote the words in 1908, the story goes after seeing a sign for a baseball game on a New York subway train, and Albert Von Tilzer wrote the music. Neither of them, it is often said, had been to a game yet. The song’s verses tell of Katie Casey, a fan who asks her boyfriend to take her to the game.
liner.tradition: Crowds sing the chorus at the seventh-inning stretch of baseball games, a custom that spread from the 1970s. Fans often swap in their own team’s name for “home team.”
